items.descriptionOriginal: Rosa Parks is known for her civil rights activism, not her cooking . But her handwritten pancake recipe is worth a look, not just as a historical document, but to see why it calls for a hearty helping of melted peanut butter. Written on the back of a bank deposit envelope, the recipe lives in the Library of Congress . On TikTok, Carlena Davis, a cook, author, and the creator of the Spilling the Sweet Tea TikTok account, tried out the recipe here and raved about it: Rosa Parks’ ‘Featherlite Pancakes’ recipe The handwritten recipe reads [edited for clarity]: Featherlite Pancakes Sift together: 1 cup flour 2 Tbsp baking powder 1/2 tsp salt 2 Tbsp sugar Mix: 1 egg 1 1/4 cup milk 1/3 cup peanut butter, melted 1 Tbsp shortening or oil Combine with dry ingredients. Cook at 275° on griddle. All in all, it’s a pretty standard pancake recipe, except for that unexpected melted peanut butter. What adding peanut butter does to a pancake recipe Many people put peanut butter on their pancakes; it’s less common to see peanut butter in the batter. What does adding peanut butter do? For one, adding peanut butter to pancakes makes them more filling. That can be great for growing kids or people who do a lot of physical work. Regular pancakes don’t have much protein or fat, so adding peanut butter beefs them up. Peanut butter also adds a rich flavor to the pancakes. Is it the secret to being “featherlite”? Perhaps. According to The Spruce , pancake texture depends on a mix of chemical reactions influenced by gas bubbles, heat, and viscosity. The fat in peanut butter could increase the pancake’s density, making it less fluffy. But it could also increase the batter’s viscosity, making it fluffier. So, it really depends on the mix of other ingredients. A woman carrying a stack of pancakes. Photo by Joy Real on Unsplash Modern peanut butter pancakes are much simpler The keto/paleo/gluten-free diet trends of the past decade have resulted in all kinds of altered recipes, some of which remove grains altogether. You can actually make a single serving of flour-free pancakes by combining: 1 small or 1/2 large banana 1 egg 1 Tbsp peanut butter 1/2 tsp baking powder Blend and cook in a pan like a regular pancake. These pancakes aren’t light and fluffy; they’re denser and crepey, but if you don’t mind a little banana-and-peanut-butter flavor, they’re quite good. (And there are lots of variations on this recipe. Some people add yogurt or cottage cheese; some use a little ground oats—they’re actually quite forgiving, so fun to experiment.) History’s recipes are often worth revisiting Today, we can find any recipe in seconds simply by Googling. Sure, you have to wade through someone’s entire life story to get to the recipe, but it’s still faster than finding the right cookbook and searching for the recipe you want. Online recipes also offer user ratings and reviews, so you can gauge how good a recipe is before you try it. However, there is something to be said for the joy of reading a recipe from someone who liked it enough to write it down by hand. There’s a story behind every envelope with a recipe written on it, like Rosa Parks’ pancakes. Did she have them at a friend’s house and ask to copy down the recipe? Did she invent it herself and finally write it out for others to copy? We may never know, but there’s something nostalgic and sweet about seeing Parks’ handwritten recipe, and even what looks like a drop of food on the envelope. You know a recipe is well-loved when it’s messy with ingredients. That’s something no online recipe can offer, no matter how long the story that accompanies it. The post Rosa Parks wrote a pancake recipe on the back of a bank envelope. One key ingredient stands out. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Hospice nurse Julie has shared tons of helpful , insightful , and even comforting videos on end-of-life care and death . Recently, she got candid about exactly what she would want to happen if she were diagnosed with dementia . She acknowledged that dementia comes in many forms and that no single approach works for everyone. But based on her years of watching patients and families navigate cognitive decline, she wanted to offer a general idea of how she would prepare. Her list included six things she would want done immediately following a diagnosis, while she still has plenty of cognitive ability to plan for such things herself. “A lot of people are gonna think this is harsh, but this is what I would want,” she said. No. 1: Establish DNR and DNI orders Hospital patient with a ‘DNR’ order. Photo credit: Canva DNR stands for “Do Not Resuscitate,” while DNI means “Do Not Intubate.” These medical orders tell healthcare providers not to do things like CPR, use a breathing tube, or use a ventilator, etc., should a patient’s heart stop beating or they stop breathing. For Julie, the decision comes down to the kind of care she would want as the dementia progresses. CPR and mechanical ventilation can be invasive, and she would prefer to allow a natural death rather than receive those interventions. No. 2: Say no to artificial nutrition Feeding tube. Photo credit: Canva Julie also said she would not want a feeding tube or to agree to assisted feeding if the dementia progressed to the point where she could not feed herself. In her view, that level of assistance would indicate that her quality of life had declined beyond what she would find acceptable. “I would rather cut my life short,” she said. According to GoodRx , studies indicate that tube feeding does not prolong life, improve quality of life, or prevent aspiration pneumonia in patients with severe dementia. They are more often designed as a temporary fix for shorter treatments, such as after a stroke, during cancer treatment, or while recovering from surgery. Julie did add the disclaimer that, in this situation, there would be a chance the disease has not advanced enough to truly mark the end of life. That means a person could be cutting their life short by starving to death and “feeling” that starvation. But in this scenario, the person would have had enough notice to be placed in hospice care and hopefully on some “comfort meds” so there wouldn’t have to be suffering. No. 3: Decline infection treatment Family surrounding man in hospital. Photo credit: Canva People with advanced dementia can develop complications such as aspiration pneumonia and urinary tract infections. If Julie found herself in this position, she would rather allow the infection to run its course than prolong her life with intense cognitive decline. Comfort-focused care options exist in these situations. For instance, administering Tylenol and morphine can manage symptoms like pain and achiness. This does not mean that infections should automatically go untreated for people with dementia. The right choice depends on the person’s preference, overall health, and care goals. No. 4: Start planning for the cost of care Older woman meeting with a financial advisor. Photo credit: Canva Julie also recommends thinking about the financial side of dementia as soon as possible. Hospice can cover many services for eligible people, including medical care, medications related to terminal illness, and support for patients and families through Medicare Part A , Medi-Cal, private insurance, or the VA. But hospice isn’t the same as round-the-clock custodial care. Generally, 24/7 care at home or room and board in a nursing facility is paid out of pocket. This makes long-term financial planning particularly important. Depending on the person’s needs and resources, care might eventually require family caregivers, paid home care, assisted living, or memory care in a skilled nursing facility. The National Institute on Aging also recommends making financial and long-term care plans early, while the person with dementia can still participate in those decisions. This ensures the individual’s voice guides critical legal and financial choices before cognitive decline limits their ability to make them. In addition to creating a budget, this includes setting up a durable power of attorney, creating a living will, and consulting an elder law attorney. No. 5: Plan the funeral Funeral. Photo credit: Canva While she can still choose for herself, Julie wants to decide whether she wants to be buried or cremated, whether she wants a funeral service, and what types of music or readings she might want included. It might feel strange to plan a funeral so far in advance, but doing so can take some of the burden off loved ones later, so they don’t have to guess. Especially if dementia eventually makes it difficult for the person to communicate these wishes. No. 6: Have a ‘living funeral’ Celebration of life. Photo credit: Canva Finally, Julie said she would want to “celebrate” her life while she could still fully participate. She knows that a dementia diagnosis would bring a natural “grieving process.” But rather than waiting until the disease had progressed, she would want to gather the people she loves and honor who she is at that moment. This could mean a big gathering or “living funeral,” as she phrased it. Or it could mean simply making more time for the people and activities that bring her joy. Whatever your wishes are, make them known For Julie, all these decisions come back to one thing: making them while she can still speak for herself. Of course, end-of-life care is a series of deeply personal decisions. A person with dementia may have very different wishes depending on their health, values, and disease stage. That’s why it’s important to discuss these choices with a doctor and loved ones while the person can still decide. That means learning about the specific diagnosis, talking with doctors and loved ones, and discussing what quality of life means to her before she may no longer be able to communicate those wishes. An advance directive can then put those preferences in writing. It lets a person document their wishes for future medical care if they become unable to make or communicate decisions. Depending on state law, it can also allow someone to designate a healthcare proxy or durable power of attorney to make medical decisions on their behalf. They can be filled out for free online. These conversations are never easy, with ourselves or with others. But having them early can give our loved ones and us clarity when it matters most. The post Hospice nurse shares the 6 things she’d do immediately after getting diagnosed with dementia appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: So you’re at a party and are introduced to someone you have never met before. How do you start the conversation? Many will ask, “What do you do for a living?” but that can make the other person uncomfortable if they feel their career isn’t terribly interesting. It also sounds a lot like you’re secretly asking: “How much money do you make?” You can also ask, “How was your day today?” but if the other person’s day was uneventful, this could be a real conversation dead-ender. The same goes for “What are you doing this weekend?” They may have no plans or feel uncomfortable sharing them. So, what question do you ask? Two guys chatting at a party. Photo credit: Canva What’s the best small talk question to ask? Terry Gross, the host of NPR’s popular Fresh Air podcast, has interviewed thousands of people, and she always asks: “So, tell me about yourself.” She says the genius of the four-word phrase is that “it allows you to start a conversation without the fear that you’re going to inadvertently make someone uncomfortable or self-conscious,” she said in a New York Times interview. “Posing a broad question lets people lead you to who they are.” The question lets the person being asked answer in a way that reflects what they really care about. It could be their profession, a hobby, or a cause they care about. Their answer will likely reflect their interests and reveal a lot about who they truly are. It also lets them avoid topics they don’t want to discuss and keeps you from making uncomfortable assumptions. If you’re preparing for interviews or think you’ll ever be asked, “Tell me about yourself,” you need to watch this. pic.twitter.com/5qf0xVMNLG — Akintola Steve (@Akintola_steve) July 26, 2026 Asking someone, “Tell me about yourself,” also plays into basic human biology. A Harvard study found that when people talk about themselves, it activates the brain region associated with rewards like food, money, and sex. We naturally enjoy talking about ourselves because it promotes social connection, and that’s what we’re trying to do with small talk, right? This question also works because studies show that when people meet someone new, they want to understand or relate to them beyond the initial context. So, say you’re at a party for a mutual friend’s birthday. The person you’ve met would also like to relate to you in another context, such as a shared interest or a professional connection. Sociologists call these “multiplex ties,” and sharing them with others is linked to greater well-being. Two women laughing together. Photo credit: Canva Be more likable with a few follow-up questions If you really want to seal the deal and make the person you’re speaking with like you, another Harvard study found that after you ask your introductory question (“Tell me about yourself”), if you ask two follow-up questions, people will rank you much more likable than if you asked the question and then turned the conversation around to yourself. Sometimes the simplest solution is the best one. You may feel a bit reluctant to ask such a simple question to kick off an interaction. But once the conversation gets flowing, you’ll have plenty of opportunities to ask thought-provoking questions and give interesting answers. It all starts with getting your conversation partner to start talking, and nothing gets people going quite like their favorite topic: themselves. The post The 4-word small talk question that will help you get through almost any situation appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Residents at the Grace Village Retirement Community are no strangers to visits from emergency workers. Unfortunately, those visits are not always for the most uplifting reasons. This week, however, members of the Kosciusko County Sheriff’s Office stopped by the residence , simply to have coffee and tea and listen to residents’ rich tapestry of stories. Winona Lake, named for the nearby lake of the same name, is home to the retirement community. It sits in Kosciusko County, just outside Warsaw, Indiana, in a region sprinkled with lakes, ponds, and rivers . Photo Credit: Grace Village Activities Team Getting pampered When members of the Kosciusko County Sheriff’s Office visited the community, residents were thrilled they had come to share some hot drinks and have a lovely chat. Some deputies even gave mini-manicures, painting residents’ nails. WNDU (16 News Now) in South Bend reported that the deputies “sat down for a little coffee and pampering during their visit, painting residents’ nails and listening to their stories.” The Sheriff’s Office shared: “It’s a reminder that serving the community isn’t just about emergency or law enforcement. Sometimes it’s as simple as showing up and leaving behind a fresh coat of nail polish.” Upworthy spoke with David O’Connor , who works with nonprofits to share their stories. He spoke with Llesenia Simpson, activities director from the senior living facility. Simpson explained how it all went down: “We reached out in September to the Kosciusko County Sheriff’s Office and spoke with Doug Light about having a few officers join our residents for coffee and conversation planning for our October calendar.” Photo Credit: Grace Village Activities Team Pumpkin muffins and coffee Simpson described a typical morning. “Our residents typically spend that coffee hour reminiscing or listening to good music together, so when Doug agreed, we knew it would be a welcomed treat. Warsaw Starbucks in front of Meijer had actually donated pumpkin muffins and coffee for our visit.” Having their nails done was already on the schedule. “The day of, it was a full house in our Healthcare activity room. Several residents had asked to have their nails done before the officers arrived, and our team was working through that list when the officers walked in, tall, in uniform, and smiling ear to ear. Every resident’s face lit up. Even residents who are usually on the quieter side were bright-eyed and fully engaged,” Simpson continued. The Sheriff got the party started. “Sheriff Jim Smith was the first to put on gloves and ask one of our residents if he could polish her nails. She was delighted and, as I recall, replied, ‘Well, you sure can!’ None of it was planned. Once Sheriff Smith started, the nail care spread across the room, with officers and residents laughing and visiting the whole time,” Simpson recalled. ‘Pretty good at painting nails’ After being told he was a natural, Sheriff Smith answered, “I have girls and grandbabies at home, so I’ve gotten pretty good at painting nails.” Smith also said, “We want the public to know that the Sheriff’s Office is here not only to protect them, but also to work alongside them. Building trust, maintaining open communication, and creating positive interactions with our citizens are all important parts of effective law enforcement. At the end of the day, we are all part of the same community, and we are committed to making Kosciusko County a safe and welcoming place to live, work, and raise a family.” View this post on Instagram Building a community Sgt. Doug Light added: “As law enforcement officers, our responsibility goes beyond enforcing the law and responding to emergencies. It’s about building relationships, showing compassion, and reminding people that they are valued members of our community. “Visiting Grace Village gives us the opportunity to connect with our senior citizens, listen to their stories, share a smile, and maybe even paint a few fingernails. Sometimes, the most meaningful thing an officer can do is simply take the time to be present and let someone know they matter.” The post Police in a small Indiana town visited a senior community and painted the residents’ nails appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Adding a personalized mRNA-based cancer vaccine to immunotherapy after surgery for high-risk melanoma reduced the risk of recurrence or death by 42%, according to results from the phase 3 INTerpath-001 trial presented at the ESMO Congress 2026. The vaccine, intismeran autogene, was given alongside pembrolizumab and compared with pembrolizumab alone.

items.title: Η Julia Stiles τιμά τον αείμνηστο Heath Ledger με τη ρουτίνα «10 Things I Hate About You» στο «DWTS»
items.titleOriginal: Julia Stiles honors the late Heath Ledger with ’10 Things I Hate About You’ routine on ‘DWTS’
items.description: Η ηθοποιός Τζούλια Στάιλς ξεσήκωσε το κοινό για άλλη μια φορά με ένα νοσταλγικό νεύμα σε έναν άλλον από τους αγαπημένους της κινηματογραφικούς ρόλους στο χθεσινοβραδινό Dancing With the Stars. Την περασμένη εβδομάδα, η Stiles παρουσίασε μια ρουτίνα αναδρομής στην ταινία της του 2001 Save the Last Dance, κερδίζοντας διθυραμβικές κριτικές. Αυτή την εβδομάδα, αναδημιουργούσε έναν εμβληματικό χορό από την ταινία της του 1999 10 Things I Hate About You ,…
items.descriptionOriginal: Actress Julia Stiles wowed the audience once again with a nostalgic nod to another of her beloved movie roles on last night’s Dancing With the Stars . Last week, Stiles performed a throwback routine to her 2001 movie Save the Last Dance , earning rave reviews. This week, she recreated an iconic dance from her 1999 movie 10 Things I Hate About You , in which she starred opposite the late Heath Ledger . Stiles and her partner, Ezra Sosa, performed a contemporary routine to Frankie Valli’s “Can’t Keep My Eyes Off You.” At the end of the performance, Stiles paid an emotional tribute to Ledger, leaving a rose as she stood before a photo of them from the film. She also surprised the DWTS audience by bringing the film’s original cast back together on the dance floor. Stiles performs “Can’t Take My Eyes Off You” In the video package before the performance, Stiles shared , “I learned a lot from Heath. He was so authentic. I have so many great memories, but I’m also sad because I really wish I could pick up the phone and be like, ‘Hey, dude. People really care about that movie. We did something special.'” After Stiles and Sosa were introduced, they began a beautifully choreographed dance to Valli’s hit famously featured in 10 Things I Hate About You . In the movie, Ledger’s character, high schooler Patrick Verona, plays the song over the loudspeaker at the school’s stadium to woo Stiles’ character, Kat Stratford. It’s a dance seared into Millennial memories, and Stiles and Sosa recreated it with sentimental flair. Stiles wore a sparkling blue dress (similar to the one she wore to prom in the film) and long, curly hair extensions that made her resemble her on-screen self. The routine copied many of Ledger’s bleacher dance moves in the film, culminating in a tearjerking tribute to the actor. View this post on Instagram Honoring Heath Ledger As the routine ended, Sosa left Stiles alone onstage, holding a red rose. She faced a large screen where a photo of Stiles and Ledger from 10 Things I Hate About You appeared. As the music faded, Stiles’ voice took over from one of the film’s most emotional and nostalgic scenes: when her character reads a poem in class about Ledger’s character. “I hate it when you’re not around, and the fact that you didn’t call. But mostly I hate the way that I don’t hate you. Not even close. Not even a little bit. Not even at all,” she says, as she places the rose at the foot of the steps for Ledger. Cast of 10 Things I Hate About You reunites After Stiles placed the rose, cast members from the film joined her on stage for an emotional ending to the performance. Actors Joseph Gordon-Levitt, Gabrielle Union, Larisa Oleynik, Andrew Keegan, and Susan May Pratt all stood with Stiles, holding hands. In a video shared on Instagram from before the show with the cast and Stiles, Union said, “We are here tonight to support our girl, Julia Stiles. She’s gonna kill it!” The performance earned roaring applause from the crowd, and the DWTS judges awarded Stiles and Sosa 36/40 points. Viewers respond The performance was a hit with 10 Things I Hate About You and Ledger fans, who shared their thoughts in the video’s comments section: “Crying the entire dance, lost it with the rose and the cast coming out. The loss of Heath hit so hard and this just brought back all the feels ” “They even incorporated Heath Ledger’s moves into the dance. I love that! And all the cast at the end… ” “OH MY GOSH! I’m SOBBING! Props to Ezra, bringing her movies to life again. He has done great work this season. Pure light and love by showcasing and recreating a small piece of filmography brilliance in a new dance. She deserved a 10s. My nostalgia cup runneth over tonight. Amazing dedication dance. Heath is looking down proud. Had to make us cry with the poem at the end. RIP Heath. ” “Joke’s on you, Julia. I had already planned on sobbing my damn eyes out today!!” “Julia you can’t have me sobbing like this. It’s not fair.” “didnt expect to see the cast there omggg im sobbing” “The end of the dance when the cast came together ” “Her prom dress ” The post Julia Stiles honors the late Heath Ledger with ’10 Things I Hate About You’ routine on ‘DWTS’ appeared first on Upworthy .

items.titleOriginal: A hairstylist with no archaeology degree solved an ancient Roman mystery scholars got wrong for centuries

Τότε ένας επαγγελματίας κομμωτής που έγινε καλόπιστος ειδικός στην «αρχαιολογία μαλλιών» τους απέδειξε ότι έκαναν λάθος. Η Janet Stephens με έδρα τη Βαλτιμόρη γοητευόταν με τα μαλλιά σε όλη της τη ζωή. Αλλά το 2001, έγινε…
items.descriptionOriginal: For generations, scholars often assumed that the intricately braided, gravity-defying updos synonymous with Roman hairstyling were achieved with wigs. Then a professional hairdresser turned bona fide “hair archaeology” specialist proved them wrong. Baltimore-based Janet Stephens had been fascinated with hair her entire life. But in 2001, she became particularly interested in ancient hairdressing. A day at the museum turned into a years-long mission While visiting The Walters Art Museum , Stephens viewed a collection of Roman busts displayed from all angles, rather than with their backs against a wall, as was customary. Being able to circle the busts helped Stephens understand the “logic” behind certain hairstyles, leading her to believe that, contrary to scholarly consensus, they weren’t the result of wigs at all but of ingenuity. At home, Stephens at first tried, and failed, to recreate the ancient styles on practice dummies, despite having access to modern styling tools. Yet as she consulted academic articles on Roman fashion and beauty for insight, she realized the authors didn’t have a practical grasp of hair dynamics. Determined to solve the mystery, Stephens committed herself to years of both hands-on experimentation and historical research. The latter was far outside her wheelhouse, especially when it came to deciphering historical texts. Still, she pushed through, using Google Translate for scholarship written in languages she didn’t read, until, in 2005, she spotted a clue no one had noticed before in a Latin dictionary citation. A single word unlocked the mystery The Latin term acus has several meanings, including “single-prong hairpin” and “needle and thread,” according to Stephens. In the context of ancient Roman hairdressing, translators had long interpreted acus to mean “single-prong hairpin.” Which, to be fair, makes sense. Single-prong hairpins couldn’t have held up these elaborate hairstyles, but they are commonly used to secure wigs. That all checks out. However, Stephens entertained the possibility that maybe, just maybe, the Romans were actually referring to the “needle and thread” meaning of acus . Sure enough, she was able to recreate these hairstyles by sewing the braids into place with a needle and thread. Just like that, a Baltimore hairstylist with zero experience in archaeology made a groundbreaking archaeological discovery. Her findings were published in the 2008 volume of the Journal of Roman Archaeology . In 2012, her video “Julia Domna: forensic hairdressing” was presented at the Archaeological Institute of America. In 2013, she became the first person to recreate the hairstyle of the Roman Vestal Virgins. Today, her YouTube channel features historical hair recreations alongside demonstrations of more modern techniques. New answers come to those who are able to ask different questions There’s so much to glean from this story. But perhaps the biggest takeaway is that to truly understand history, we need to view it through both an academic and a practical lens. It’s also a wonderful example of how our own life experiences can give us unique insight into seemingly unrelated subjects in surprising ways. This article originally appeared in July. It has been updated. The post A hairstylist with no archaeology degree solved an ancient Roman mystery scholars got wrong for centuries appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: There are kitten lovers …and then there are Ricky’s grandparents. When Izzie Grass left her kitten , Ricky, with her parents for two weeks, she had no idea what was in store for her after she got him back. Not only had Ricky been well taken care of, but his adventures with his human grandparents were fully documented in a photobook created by Grass’s mother, which she titled “Ricky Goes to Gramma’s and Grampa’s.” The photo album that reads like a children’s book first went viral when Grass shared it on TikTok in 2020, and it has resurfaced repeatedly since, with people clamoring for more riveting Ricky content after reading about how the kitten “helped Gramma do the dishes” and how “Cousin Jasper and Charlie ate most of” the pancakes Gramma made for him. Check out how adorably extra Gramma is: The comments speak for themselves Has any kitten ever been more loved? “I would die for Ricky, Gramma, and Grampa,” wrote one commenter. “This is GOLD. I want to see ‘Ricky Learns to Drive,'” wrote another. “My parents didn’t even put this much effort into making scrapbooks for ME,” shared another. And apparently Grass isn’t the only one with pet grandparents who are a little extra. “My mom made a full year calendar of my dog after only watching her for two days,” a commenter wrote. Grass told Newsweek that her mom told her she made the book because “that’s what she does,” adding, “She is known for creating very sentimental gifts.” But Ricky almost didn’t make it at all Grass also shared that the book almost didn’t get made because Ricky almost didn’t make it as a kitten. He was brought to the veterinary clinic where Grass worked when he was 9 weeks old to be euthanized. “The individuals who dropped him off reported that they found a kitten with broken legs and that was throwing up everything they tried to feed him,” she said. “I came back from my lunch early to care for this kitten and in the kennel was Ricky.” As it turned out, Ricky had some birth defects and health problems that required specialized care, but he didn’t need to be euthanized. Grass took him home but needed a little time to prepare to give him the care he needed. “My mom stepped up and offered to watch him for a couple weeks while I got a handle of my schedule,” Grass told Newsweek . “It was during this time that she created the book.” The fact that Ricky had specialized care needs at the time makes Gramma’s photobook all the more endearing. “He has made so much progress,” Grass told Newsweek. “His esophagus works significantly better, he has learned how to walk, climb and run, and he continues to help me raise other foster kittens. Ricky is very loved and lives the life he deserved to have.” With a mom and grandparents like he has, it’s not a surprise. About those unusual paws in the photos Of course, the internet’s going to internet, and some people apparently looked at Ricky’s photobook a couple of years after the fact and complained that it was AI generated because of the way Ricky’s paws looked. However, as Grass shared in a video in 2024, those paws aren’t due to AI. They’re just Ricky’s real-life deformities that, ironically, make him appear AI-generated in the photobook. (It’s also worth mentioning that the photobook video came out well before AI-generated technology became available to the masses.) “Ricky’s legs are actually shaped like candy canes,” Grass explains. “That’s not AI. That’s inbreeding. Spay and neuter your cats.” You can find more videos of Ricky and the animals Grass fosters on her TikTok channel here . This article originally appeared three years ago and has been updated. The post Gramma and Grampa’s photobook after spending 2 weeks watching Ricky the kitten is everything appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: A viral video has been making the rounds lately that shows a giant ship opening up at its middle and dropping tons upon tons of cinderblocks directly into the ocean . The video is fascinating, so much so that I was certain it was AI-generated at first. After all, what kind of ship can part down the middle like that? Turns out, the video is real! The ship is called a split hopper barge and is often used to transport and deliver dredged soil. Dumping concrete like this looks like the world’s worst case of littering , but in actuality, the concrete blocks serve an important purpose that benefits sea life of all varieties. But how? Dumping concrete block in the ocean. Soon coral and algae will take root on them and help them create a reef. pic.twitter.com/IgEiMb3HhP — non aesthetic things (@PicturesFoIder) July 24, 2025 Why dump concrete in the ocean? For answers, look no further than the GARP , that’s the Grenada Artificial Reef Project (also known as the Grand Anse Artificial Reef Project or GAARP). With coral reefs under threat and disappearing all over the world, the team behind the project came up with an interesting solution they wanted to test out. In 2013, Phil Saye, owner of the Dive Grenada dive shop , and his team began placing concrete pyramids (basically, cinderblocks stacked together into something of a tower structure) in a barren part of the Caribbean Sea. The location was just off the coastal beaches of Grenada. View this post on Instagram The pyramids filled up fast In just 3 months, the pyramids had attracted tons of marine life. The block pyramids gave shelter to the animals who otherwise had nowhere to hide, nest, or feed in this part of the water. “An initial growth of algae and colourful encrusting sponge was soon followed by a varied range of invertebrates. These included feather duster worms, lobster, crab, and urchins. Excitement developed as we started to see a range of juvenile fish including squirrel fish, goat fish, grunts and scorpionfish,” says the official website. After a year, word must have spread among the fish, because the simple concrete blocks transformed into “buzzing diverse communit[ies] of marine life.” At around 18 months, things started to get really exciting. Stony and brain corals, described as the “building blocks of coral” began to appear on the pyramids. In the years since, the project has exploded with more and more coral growing on the blocks and more fish and other sea life moving in. “Each subsequent year more pyramids have been added to increase biomass. GARP is becoming a balanced ecosystem, home to over 30 species of fish, 14 different kinds of corals and many of the invertebrates and algae you would find on a naturally occurring reef,” the project’s website says. A peer-reviewed 2024 study found the pyramids resemble natural reefs in many respects but differ significantly in macroalgae and coralline algae cover. Today, there are about 100 pyramids in the location, each built from 30 cinder blocks. Other, similar projects are taking place in waterways all over the globe. GARP/GAARP isn’t the first or only project of its kind. Concrete has been shown again and again to make an excellent shelter for marine life and a perfect launching pad for new coral growth. Not every reef experiment works People have tried other materials before, to varied results. One such project off the coast of Florida in the 1970s utilized utilized an estimated one to two million (!) old tires in an effort to create new fish habitats. Called the Osborne Reef, the effort is now considered a major ecological disaster as storms and sea currents have tossed many of the tires around, washing them ashore and even damaging otherwise healthy natural reefs nearby. Talk about a backfire. Major cleanup efforts to undo the damage are still underway: Florida’s Department of Environmental Protection has removed more than half a million tires so far, and roughly the same number are still on the seabed. Specialized concrete structures are heavy enough to stay put in rough conditions and are one of the few things that can withstand years and years of being battered by rough, salty seawater without degrading. Coral reefs are disappearing around the globe at an alarming rate. Physical damage, both natural and manmade, along with pollution, coral harvesting, global warming, and bleaching wreaks havoc on natural ecosystems under the sea. Coral reefs aren’t just there to look pretty. They dampen waves and currents before they hit land, reducing erosion and protecting people who live on the coast. Reefs are home to a huge variety of marine life who use it for shelter and finding food. And, finally, they’re amazing destinations for scientific discovery, new species and even medical treatments are being discovered on reefs all the time! All of that is at risk, because the very existence of coral reefs may be in jeopardy. The EPA calls rising ocean temperatures and changing ocean chemistry the greatest global threats to reefs, and NOAA says bleaching-level heat stress during the fourth global mass bleaching event, which ran from early 2023 to mid-2025, hit 84% of the world’s coral reef area . A landmark 2025 report also concluded that warm-water coral reefs have crossed a critical tipping point. The ocean needs more than concrete There’s no easy fix to this grave problem. Natural coral reefs take thousands of years to grow and mature. So, even with all the cinderblocks in the world acting as growth platforms, it would be impossible for us to replace all the coral we’ve already killed or destroyed. Saving our oceans must be a multi-faceted effort, with initiatives that combat pollution and rising sea temperatures in addition to creating artificial reefs. But projects like GARP/GAARP are an awesome start. They may not save the planet all on their own, but if you ask me, those fish look pretty darn grateful for their new home. This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post Scientists left cinderblocks in a barren part of the sea. 3 months later they were ecstatic. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: A research team led by professor Minhae Kwon of the School of Electronic and Electrical Engineering has developed two core next-generation artificial intelligence (AI) technologies that enable AI systems to handle complex, long-horizon tasks more effectively while reducing computational costs and improving safety. The findings address key challenges that have hindered the commercialization of costly AI assistant services as well as the deployment of AI in safety-critical areas such as robotics and autonomous driving. The findings are published on the arXiv preprint server.

Η τεχνολογία εφευρέθηκε από μια ομάδα επιστημόνων στο Κορεατικό Ινστιτούτο Ενεργειακής Έρευνας (KIER) που εδρεύει στο Daejeon. Επικεφαλής της προσπάθειας ήταν ο SeJin Ahn, PhD…
items.descriptionOriginal: A new catalytic process developed by South Korean researchers could extend the lifespan of perovskite solar cells by preserving 95 percent of their initial efficiency after 1,000 hours of testing. The technology was invented by a group of scientists at the Daejeon-based Korea Institute of Energy Research (KIER). The effort was led by SeJin Ahn, PhD, a faculty member and principal researcher at the institute. The team also collaborated with a group led by Dong-Seok Kim, PhD, at the Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology (UNIST). For the initiative, the cells were tested at temperatures of 185 degrees Fahrenheit (85 degrees Celsius) and 85 percent relative humidity. Still, even after 1,000 hours of exposure to extreme heat and humidity, they retained 95 percent of their initial power conversion efficiency. According to the team, the new process could help perovskite solar cells compete with traditional silicon panels. “By solving the chronic lifetime issue, it will become an important milestone toward the commercialization of perovskite and tandem solar cells,” Ahn emphasized. Longer-lasting solar cells Perovskite solar cells are thin-film photovoltaic devices, which rely on perovskite materials to convert sunlight into electricity. They have attracted a great deal of attention in recent years because of their high energy conversion efficiency and potential for a low-cost manufacturing. They are also cheap, easy to produce, and lightweight, which makes them suitable for flexible solar panels. But their lifespan is limited ranging from two to 10 years, compared with 25 to 30 years for silicon panels . They are also particularly vulnerable to heat and moisture, which can accelerate their degradation. Solar cell sample applying the novel catalytic process technology developed by the Korea Institute of Energy Research (KIER). Credit: KIER This reduces their long-term reliability, especially in hot and humid climates. The problem stems from lithium salts and additives in the hole transport layer. While these substances improve the cells’ efficiency, they also accelerate degradation. In hot and humid conditions, the additives can evaporate , leaving tiny gaps in the thin film that reduce performance. At the same time, lithium ions can move freely inside the cell, and cause further damage and shortening its lifespan. Until now, researchers have struggled to eliminate these substances without compromising the cells’ ability to convert sunlight into electricity. New catalytic process To tackle the issue, the KIER team’s new catalytic process called the post-catalytic reaction filtering extraction process. The method removes harmful lithium ions and eliminates the need for additives while maintaining high power conversion efficiency. The technology uses a nickel oxide (NiOx) catalyst . It attracts and removes lithium ions from the solution used to create the hole transport layer. When added to the solution, the nickel oxide powder undergoes a reaction that changes its surface properties, thus allowing it to attract lithium ions. The reaction separates lithium ions from the salt without chemical additives. The released ions then attach to the nickel oxide particles. The researchers then use a physical filtration process to remove the powder from the solution. Because the nickel oxide particles are relatively large, they become trapped in the filter, and remove the attached lithium ions with them. Researchers performing performance tests of the technology. Credit: KIER This results in a purified solution free of additives, residual lithium, and catalyst, which can be used to produce a defect-free hole transport layer. The catalyst is then removed. To evaluate the technology, the team tested solar cells made with the new process and compared them with conventional cells. As outlined, the technology greatly preserve the cells’ performance. However, the new cells also achieved 25.24 percent efficiency, which is slightly higher than the 25.21 percent of conventional cells made with additives. According to the team, this findings could improve tandem solar cells. “This work is significant in that it breaks away from the conventional framework for perovskite fabrication and presents a new process that catalytically induces only the necessary reactions and then filters out the root-cause substances,” Ahn concluded in a press release . The study has been published in the journal Advanced Science .

items.descriptionOriginal: Retirement can mean many things to different Americans. It can mean aging in place while relying on Social Security and eking by on a fixed income, or it could mean moving to a lavish retirement community . It can mean picking up part-time work to get by or stay active, or traveling the world with a partner, and everything in between. What retirement doesn’t usually mean is moving back into a glorified “college dorm” and hanging out with 20-year-olds in your spare time. But Arizona State University and Pacific Retirement Services figured the idea was just wild enough to work. ASU opens “Mirabella,” an on-campus retirement community, in 2020 In 2013, Arizona State University President Michael Crow had the idea that college wasn’t and shouldn’t only be for 18-year-olds coming out of high school. Night classes or supplemental learning for adults of all ages and backgrounds would no longer be an afterthought, but a major part of the school culture. He called this vision the “ New American University .” Instead of measuring prestige by how many students the school rejected, they’d measure how many different kinds of students they could include. As part of that concept, the university’s development arm partnered with Pacific Retirement Services to develop a retirement community that would not just be close to campus, it would be a part of it. Research suggested that when seniors had community engagement, purpose, and intergenerational contact, they had better health and cognitive outcomes. This new community, part of a growing trend of University Based Retirement Communities (UBRCs) would put that idea to the test, and into action. In 2020, the building, named “Mirabella,” officially opened. Mirabella at ASU was built in 2020. Photo Credit: Wikimedia Commons Campus retirement home unites old and young students, to everyone’s benefit Mirabella isn’t your average retirement community that just happens to be near one of the most vibrant and exciting college campuses in the country. Residents don’t have to be former ASU students to live at Mirabella, but many of them are; and they’re overjoyed to be back at their alma mater among so many memories. No matter where the residents come from, however, all residents are officially Sun Devils and receive official student ID cards that let them access all of the campus amenities. Seniors over 62 who live at Mirabella can audit classes on campus, go to sporting events and games, access the library; you name it. It keeps them engaged in the community directly around them, protects their brains from cognitive decline, and organically reduces loneliness. But perhaps the most incredible thing about the concept is the intergenerational contact it creates. Residents volunteer and mentor students on campus, imparting their years of wisdom and experience on the younger generation. Within the halls of Mirabella, some graduate design and arts students live free of charge; they’re only asked to put on performances and workshops for the residents. Which they do gladly. One beautiful example of this connection in action is the All Ears Friendship Bench. It’s a program run by Mirabella that places a resident volunteer on a bench on a prominent part of campus. There, they simply sit and offer a kind ear, advice, wisdom, and friendship to anyone who happens to need it as they pass by. “I find it energizing, and I feel like I’m helping them,” a volunteer said, per ASU . “One girl told me, ‘I’ve only been here 15 minutes, but I feel so much better.” Mirabella is expensive and exclusive, but it works Mirabella is a state of the art facility that comes with numerous perks and amenities for residents. That means space is limited, and the price tag is steep . Quite a bit more than your standard senior living home. Simply put, a community like this is not in reach for most retirees. There have also been reports of some tension and clashes within the campus community. ASU’s reputation as a “party school” is well-earned, and not all of the residents are fans of the nonstop activity and loud music . That could be because the building is located directly next to Shady Park Tempe, a live outdoor music venue. Shady Park was forced via lawsuits to install sound abatement structures to dampen the noise, much to the chagrin of some students. But, all things considered, the model is exciting and promising. A case study published in the Journal of Aging and Environment lauded the benefits of such a community: “Well-designed UBRCs can be an effective mechanism for increasing intergenerational connections that offer opportunities to create mutual understanding between younger and older adults. Exposing younger individuals to older persons may support positive views of aging … in alignment with the World Health Organization’s strategies for reducing ageism … This learning experience is reciprocal, in that older persons also learn new skills and perspectives while interacting with younger individuals.” Ideas to make UBRCs like Mirabella more accessible include shifting to a rental pricing structure versus buying in for life, having residents live in dedicated sections of existing dorms, or even offering all of the programs and benefits to seniors who live off-campus in more affordable housing. UBRCs like Mirabella are becoming more popular. There are already dozens of them at colleges around the country—including Berry College, Duke, Penn State, and the University of Florida. As the promising data and first-hand accounts continue to pour in, it could be something we see a whole lot more of. It’s a totally new and exciting way to think about how we retire and age. One resident put it beautifully on Google reviews: “There is energy here! We volunteer, attend classes, develop student friendships, cheer at recitals and sporting events, and learn/share stories. We are people who love learning and reject being isolated into an ‘old people’s’ community. Wouldn’t you?” The post Retired former ASU students are moving back to campus. The experiment is a wild success. appeared first on Upworthy .

Ο Christoph Landolt αντλεί από την εικόνα αυτού του Red Queen's Race για να περιγράψει την κατάσταση του soft…
items.descriptionOriginal: In Lewis Carroll's "Alice Through the Looking Glass," the eponymous heroine encounters the Red Queen, who involves her in a frantic race. In this curious country, Alice learns, you have to run as fast as you possibly can only to remain in the same place. Christoph Landolt draws on the image of this Red Queen's Race to describe the situation of software vendors in the AI era. As the cyber capabilities of frontier models continue to grow, the potential for attacks is multiplying at speed too. Using an approach from game theory, Landolt and his co-authors have calculated how the release of new AI models could be sequenced to give software vendors a strategic head start over cybercriminals.

items.descriptionOriginal: Stepping up efforts to develop battery-free sensors, U.S. researchers have created a graphene-based device that harvests energy from ambient radiation to provide the electricity needed to operate an ultra-low-power temperature sensor. The technology lets the sensor operate for at least 24 hours during a power outage. The latest prototype is the team’s second self-powered sensor, following an earlier graphene-based solar-powered sensor. Together, the two devices are part of a wider effort to create autonomous sensors that draw energy from multiple sources in their surroundings instead of relying on conventional batteries. Harvests local energy The research, carried out by physicists and materials scientists at the University of Arkansas and the University of Michigan, is aimed at meeting three key requirements for next-generation sensors . According to the team, the devices must harvest energy locally, consume only nanowatts of power, and operate unattended for years, potentially decades. The researchers said the latest ambient radiation-powered sensor satisfies all three criteria. As opposed to traditional wireless sensors that depend on batteries, the new device captures energy already present in everyday environments. Paul Thibado, a physics professor at the University of Arizona who began studying the properties of Graphene nearly a decade ago, said ambient electromagnetic radiation exists throughout modern homes because of electrical wiring. The sensor uses a graphene inductor to harvest energy from the magnetic fields surrounding power lines. That energy is then sent through a circuit, converted into usable electricity, and stored in capacitors that power the temperature sensor, he added. Thibado further explained that because the capacitors are replenished faster than they are discharged, the sensor can continue operating even if power is interrupted. “The inductor adds charge to these capacitors at a slow rate, but it’s faster than the rate the sensor uses up the charges from the capacitors,” he added. According to Thibado, the stored energy can keep the sensor running for at least 24 hours during a power outage and potentially as long as a week, depending on operating conditions. Cost-effective, sustainable Besides the longer operation hours, the battery-free design also reduces the need for routine maintenance. Since the sensors do not require battery replacements, they can lower maintenance costs, labor, and battery waste. Thibado, in a statement, described the approach as “set it and forget it,” noting that eliminating battery changes makes the sensors easier to deploy in locations where routine maintenance is difficult. While the researchers demonstrated the technology using a temperature sensor, they hope to expand the applications for these self-controlled sensing systems. Potential uses include monitoring products during shipping, tracking environmental conditions such as soil and atmospheric temperature, managing logistics fleets, wearable fitness devices, and healthcare monitoring systems. Going forward, the team plans to combine several graphene-based energy-harvesting technologies into a single sensor. Beyond ambient radiation, future devices could draw energy from sunlight, heat, sound, motion, and other environmental sources. Using multiple energy sources would allow the sensors to continue operating if one source becomes unavailable, improving dependability during power outages or other interruptions. The researchers believe such multi-source, self-powered sensors could operate for decades with little or no maintenance, helping expand the Internet of Things (IoT) by enabling long-lasting smart devices that function autonomously without batteries. ​

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News 5 Sustainable Swaps You Can Make Around Your Home Today Reading Time: 2 minutes 5 Sustainable Swaps You Can Make Around Your Home Today Making your home more sustainable doesn’t require expensive renovations or a complete lifestyle overhaul. In fact, some of the most effective changes are surprisingly simple, and you can start making them today. From the products you use to clean your kitchen to the materials you sleep under, everyday household choices can affect the environment. If you want to reduce waste, embrace more natural materials, and make your home a little greener, here are five sustainable swaps to consider. 1. Swap Disposable Cleaning Products for Reusable Alternatives Consider how many paper towels, disposable wipes, and plastic cleaning bottles you use in a typical month. These everyday essentials can create surprising waste, especially when you replace them constantly. Instead, consider switching to washable microfiber cloths, reusable cleaning pads, and refillable spray bottles . You can also explore concentrated cleaning solutions that require less packaging and are designed to be diluted at home. These small changes can reduce household waste while helping you save money over time. 2. Choose Natural Bedding Over Synthetic Materials Your bedroom is another great place to introduce more sustainable materials, especially in your bedding. Many conventional comforters contain synthetic polyester fillings derived from petroleum-based materials, which can contribute to plastic pollution. Replacing them with natural alternatives is a more environmentally conscious choice. An organic wool comforter offers a natural filling that provides warmth while allowing air to circulate and helping regulate temperature throughout the night. Wool is also renewable and biodegradable when untreated, making it an appealing option for anyone looking to reduce reliance on synthetic textiles. Your bedroom is a great place to introduce sustainable materials, especially in your bedding. Image: Home of Wool 3. Replace Single-Use Kitchen Products The kitchen is often one of the biggest sources of household waste, but it’s also one of the easiest places to make sustainable improvements. Instead of relying on plastic wrap, disposable sandwich bags, and single-use food containers, invest in reusable alternatives. Glass storage containers, washable silicone bags, and beeswax food wraps can help you cut down on unnecessary packaging. You could also swap disposable coffee pods for a reusable coffee filter or French press. Over time, these changes can noticeably reduce how much waste leaves your kitchen. 4. Switch to Energy-Efficient Lighting If you’re still using traditional incandescent light bulbs, switching to LED alternatives is a straightforward way to reduce household energy consumption. LED bulbs use significantly less electricity and generally last much longer than incandescent bulbs, so you need to replace them less often. This can help lower both your electricity bills and your home’s environmental footprint. You can also make better use of natural daylight by keeping windows unobstructed and arranging furniture to maximize available sunlight. 5. Choose Refillable Bathroom Essentials Bathrooms can quickly accumulate plastic packaging, particularly from shampoo, conditioner, hand soap, and body wash bottles. Switch to refillable products or solid alternatives, such as shampoo bars and bar soaps. Many brands now offer concentrated refills, so you can reuse existing containers instead of buying new plastic bottles every time. You might also replace disposable cotton rounds with washable alternatives and choose toothbrushes with replaceable heads to cut unnecessary waste. Start with one or two manageable swaps, build on them gradually, and you’ll soon discover that sustainable living can be both practical and rewarding. The post 5 Sustainable Swaps You Can Make Around Your Home Today appeared first on Happy Eco News .

Στην πραγματικότητα, το 39% του παγκόσμιου αντιμονίου χρησιμοποιείται για τη δημιουργία επιβραδυντικού φλόγας…
items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers have developed a new way to quickly recycle electronic waste. Many electronic devices use flame-retardant plastic as casing in order to reduce the risk of electrical fires. This plastic is formulated using a metal called antimony along with organic bromide compounds. In fact, 39% of the world’s antimony is used to create flame-retardant plastics, most of which will eventually end up as part of the tens of millions of tons of electronic waste generated each year. Rice University’s James Tour recently published a study in Nature Chemical Engineering detailing an improved method to recover antimony from this electronic waste stream. “Antimony is a critical metal with a constrained supply,” says Tour, a professor of chemistry and corresponding author on the study. “My research team has adapted our flash Joule heating technique to quickly and effectively recover antimony from this plastic waste stream.” To recapture antimony from the plastic, it first has to be released from the plastic. This is, chemically, a challenging step. As the antimony is released, other toxic compounds, organic bromides, can form that are difficult to capture. “Conventionally heating the plastic releases the antimony in a volatile and difficult to collect form as well as creating and releasing hazardous organic bromide compounds,” says Leo Haoxin Ye, the first author of this paper and a graduate student at Rice. “Other options are risky or more impractical, such as using strong acids, organic solvents, or multistep treatment options.” The issue, the team thought, could be with the slowness of conventional heating, which allowed the elements to change forms or create new compounds. If they could adapt Tour’s flash Joule heating, which heats materials up to hundreds of degrees Celsius in a manner of milliseconds, they might be able to avoid some of the pitfalls of conventional heating while still releasing the antimony from the plastic. “We found flame-retardant plastic waste generated by our own laboratory, ground it up, and then placed it between two sheets of electrically heated carbon paper. We used ultrafast heating to pulse-heat it several times,” Ye says. “Then we held the plastic briefly at a high temperature, which allowed the antimony to evaporate and condense in a collection area.” The method, called isothermal-clamped flash Joule heating, was tested on three different types of flame-retardant plastic: a power-supply housing, a printed circuit board, and an electrical connector. From these, the team was able to recover approximately 90% of the antimony, while converting 83% of the bromide into hydrogen bromide, an inorganic compound that, while hazardous, is a valuable industrial chemical that can be captured with sodium hydroxide to form a stable salt. And the number of organic bromide compounds produced dramatically reduced, a result of the flash Joule heating’s speed. The plastic spent only 9.4 milliseconds in between 200-500 degrees Celsius, the temperature range in which organic bromide compounds form. “Isothermal-clamped flash Joule heating could improve the speed, safety, and practicality of antimony recovery from discarded flame-retardant plastics,” Tour says. “Given that the world is on track to produce 82 million metric tons of flame-retardant plastic waste by 2030, this represents an important step forward to conserving and reusing our critical antimony supply while also regenerating bromide salts for reuse.” This research was funded by the Air Force Office of Scientific Research and the US Army Corps of Engineers, ERDC. Source: Rice University The post New method can quickly recycle electronic waste appeared first on Futurity .

items.title: Τα ανθρώπινα νευρικά βλαστοκύτταρα είναι ευαίσθητα στις παραλλαγές του ιού COVID
items.titleOriginal: Human neural stem cells are susceptible to COVID virus variants
items.description: Τα ανθρώπινα νευρικά βλαστοκύτταρα που βοηθούν στο σχηματισμό του εγκεφάλου και του νωτιαίου μυελού είναι πολύ ευαίσθητα στον SARS-CoV-2, συμπεριλαμβανομένων των παραλλαγών BA.1 και BA.2 του Omicron, σύμφωνα με νέα έρευνα. Τα ευρήματα εγείρουν ανησυχίες σχετικά με τις πιθανές επιπτώσεις της μητρικής λοίμωξης COVID-19 στην πρώιμη ανάπτυξη του νευρικού συστήματος και υπογραμμίζουν τη σημασία της παρακολούθησης των παιδιών πρώην…
items.descriptionOriginal: Human neural stem cells that help form the brain and spinal cord are highly susceptible to SARS-CoV-2, including Omicron variants BA.1 and BA.2, according to new research. The findings raise concerns about the potential effects of maternal COVID-19 infection on early nervous system development and underscore the importance of monitoring children exposed to the virus before birth. The researchers, led by Prue Talbot, a professor of the graduate division in the Department of Molecular, Cell and Systems Biology, found that human neural stem cells were significantly more susceptible to infection by SARS-CoV-2 spike pseudoparticles—modified, non-replicating virus particles used to safely study infection—than undifferentiated human embryonic stem cells. The susceptibility was observed with the original viral spike as well as the two Omicron variants. “Our data clearly show that human neural stem cells are readily infected by SARS-CoV-2 pseudovirus, including the currently prevalent Omicron variants,” Talbot says. Neural stem cells emerge from the ectoderm, an early embryonic tissue that gives rise to the central nervous system. Because these cells help establish the foundation for the brain and spinal cord, infection during early development could have consequences ranging from pregnancy loss and severe developmental abnormalities to more subtle changes that may not be apparent at birth. “Such subtle damage might only appear years later as learning, behavioral, or cognitive difficulties,” says Ann Song, a postdoctoral researcher in Talbot’s lab and the first author of the study in PLOS One . The transmission of SARS-CoV-2 from mother to fetus has been documented, including during the first trimester. Children exposed to the virus in utero are now reaching ages at which potential neurodevelopmental differences can be assessed. The researchers also noted that their findings are consistent with a large health-record study linking maternal SARS-CoV-2 infection to an increased risk of a neurodevelopmental diagnosis in children by age 3. To investigate how the virus might enter developing neural cells, the team differentiated human embryonic stem cells into neural stem cells and exposed them to the pseudoparticles. The experiments showed that Omicron pseudoparticles entered neural stem cells primarily through endocytosis, a process in which cells engulf external material. The researchers found that blocking this pathway with the compound filipin reduced viral entry by approximately 75% to 85%. The team also found that neural stem cells have a relatively sparse layer of sugar molecules on their surfaces. Removing these sugar groups increased pseudoparticle entry twofold to fourfold, suggesting that the cell-surface sugar layer may help limit viral access. The research addresses a question that cannot readily be investigated through experiments in pregnant women: whether early precursors of the nervous system are vulnerable to SARS-CoV-2. Although fetal transmission has been documented, the susceptibility of these early developmental cells has been less clear. “Our data emphasize the need for monitoring children exposed in utero to SARS-CoV-2 for evidence of deficiencies in the central nervous system,” Song says. Talbot says the findings do not establish that infection of neural stem cells by the pseudovirus causes neurological harm in human pregnancies. “Further research will be needed to determine whether and how infection at these early stages affects brain development,” she says. The study was funded by a UCR Academic Senate Committee on Research grant, an Academic Merit Fellowship, a Yvonne Danielson Endowed Graduate Award, a UCR Graduate Division Dissertation Completion Fellowship Award, and the Tobacco-Related Disease Research Program. Source: UC Riverside The post Human neural stem cells are susceptible to COVID virus variants appeared first on Futurity .

items.descriptionOriginal: He’s the first Indian to win the Oskar Klein Medal, yet he still cycles to work. His story is as much about simplicity as it is about extraordinary scientific achievement. Meet Kolkata-born theoretical physicist Ashoke Sen, whose pioneering research in string theory and black hole physics has helped shape our understanding of the universe. After studying at Presidency College and IIT Kanpur and pursuing doctoral research in the United States, he returned to India to continue his scientific journey. In 2012, Sen received the $3 million Fundamental Physics Prize for his contributions to string theory. In 2026, he made history by becoming the first Indian physicist to receive the Oskar Klein Medal, recognising his influential work in theoretical physics. Despite global recognition and some of the field’s highest honours, Sen’s story reminds us that scientific greatness is measured by curiosity, dedication and the ideas we contribute, not by outward displays of success. His journey continues to inspire young Indians to pursue knowledge and push the boundaries of human understanding. Know a student who’s drawn to physics? items.titleOriginal: 'I Spent 4 Years Farming on Weekends. Here Are 7 Things to Know Before Starting Your Own Organic Farm'
items.description: Για χρόνια, ο Deepak Sabharwal γνώριζε το φαγητό σε μεγάλο βαθμό από την άλλη πλευρά του τραπεζιού. Είχε περάσει σχεδόν δύο δεκαετίες στον εταιρικό κόσμο, συνεργαζόμενος με εταιρείες όπως η General Electric (GE), η PepsiCo και η Tata. Οι μέρες του αφορούσαν συναντήσεις, αριθμούς και ανάπτυξη. Η γεωργία ήταν κάτι που περνούσε χρόνο κάνοντας τα Σαββατοκύριακα, στις φάρμες της οικογένειάς του στο Pushkar, R.…
items.descriptionOriginal: For years, Deepak Sabharwal knew food largely from the other side of the table. He had spent nearly two decades in the corporate world, working with companies such as General Electric (GE), PepsiCo, and Tata. His days were about meetings, numbers, and growth. Farming was something he spent time doing on weekends, at his family's farms in Pushkar, Rajasthan. Then one day, he noticed the pesticides being used on his own farm . Around the same time, his mother was diagnosed with cancer. The two things came together in his mind in a way he could not ignore. "I began wondering what we were really eating every day, and that was a simple but uncomfortable question to ask," he tells The Better India . That question eventually took him from boardrooms to fields. His hands-on farming journey began in 2012, while he was still working at GE, and he spent almost four years travelling to Pushkar on weekends to learn farming and experiment on his family's land. Today, he is based in Delhi NCR and is the co-founder and CEO of Earthy Tales Organics Private Limited . The company was formally started in December 2018 with a focus on natural farming, farmer livelihoods, and making produce grown without synthetic pesticides and fertilisers more accessible to urban families. Deepak wanted Earthy Tales to do more than sell vegetables. For the co-founder, it was about fixing a disconnect he had begun to see between the soil, the farmer, and the person eventually eating the food. Years of working closely with farmers taught him that organic farming involves much more than avoiding synthetic pesticides and fertilisers. Here are seven lessons he wishes anyone entering the space would understand. 1. Start with the soil It is tempting to begin a farming business by asking one question. What should I grow? Deepak believes there is another question that should come first. What is the condition of my soil? Today, Deepak is based in Delhi NCR and is the co-founder and CEO of Earthy Tales Organics Private Limited. Before investing heavily, he advises testing the soil and water, understanding what was previously grown on the land, and finding out which chemicals may have been used there. Because for him, organic farming does not begin with a label. It begins underground. "Organic farming begins with soil, not with certification or branding," he says. A healthy farm may require compost, organic matter, mulching, natural inputs, better water management and, where appropriate, livestock integration. The aim is to move away from synthetic pesticides and fertilisers while gradually rebuilding the health of the land. That is also why he advises beginners not to convert an entire farm at once. He suggests starting with a small patch, trying a crop and observing how it performs over one or two cycles before taking the bigger plunge. After all, the soil has its own pace. A business plan cannot always make it move faster. 2. Build the whole system One of his early assumptions was that organic farming was largely about avoiding synthetic pesticides and fertilisers. He soon realised how incomplete that understanding was. Seed selection, soil health, water, compost, livestock, pest management, crop planning, harvesting, grading, storage, and transport all become part of the equation. "Natural farming is not only about not using chemicals. It is a complete system," he says. And the work does not end when the crop leaves the field. It has to be sorted, packed, and transported. Some produce will be damaged. Some will not look perfect. Some may not sell in time. All of that has a cost. For someone starting, this is an important reality to understand. You are not simply starting a farm. You are building a system around that farm. 3. Earn farmer trust Getting a farmer to change the way they have farmed for years is not as easy as giving them a training session. Deepak learnt this by working closely with farmers. A farmer cannot treat a crop as an experiment. A crop failure can mean a family's income is affected. So when someone asks a farmer to reduce their reliance on synthetic pesticides or change farming practices, the farmer needs more than promises. "Farmers do not trust speeches. They trust consistency," he adds. The aim is not only to stop using chemicals, but to gradually rebuild the health of the land. That consistency can mean repeated visits to the farm, helping identify pests, discussing what to do when a crop begins to fail , providing training and, most importantly, helping create a market for what the farmer grows. At Earthy Tales, the approach has involved working closely with farmers and supporting them in moving towards natural farming methods that rely less on synthetic inputs. The lesson is particularly important for entrepreneurs who want to work with farmers. If you want farmers to take a risk with you, you have to be willing to share some of that risk. 4. Find buyers first This was another lesson that took the co-founder time to learn. In farming, it is easy to fall in love with the idea of growing something. But a good crop does not automatically become a good business. "Natural farming must be market-linked. Otherwise, the farmer carries all the risk," he says. So before sowing, an entrepreneur needs to think about the customer. What does the customer buy regularly? What can the region grow reliably? What price is realistic? How far does the produce need to travel? Who will buy it? At Earthy Tales, he noticed that many customers first came looking for fresh fruits and vegetables. Once they developed confidence in the source, they began buying everyday staples such as atta, pulses, oils, spices, and ghee. The company was formally started in December 2018 with a focus on natural farming, farmer livelihoods, and making chemical-free food more accessible to urban families. That taught him something important about building a food business. Trust usually comes before the larger basket. A farmer may produce something excellent. But if there is no reliable buyer at the other end, the farmer still carries the risk. The market, therefore, cannot be an afterthought. It has to be part of the crop plan from the beginning. 5. Plan for uncertainty This sounds obvious, but it is one of the hardest realities for a business-minded newcomer to accept. Nature does not work according to demand forecasts. A farmer can plan for a crop, only for rain, heat, pests, or disease to change the outcome. Even when the crop does well, demand may not arrive at the same pace. Deepak remembers believing in the early days that good produce would naturally find its way to customers. "I believed that if we had good produce, the rest would follow," he says. "But food does not work like that." A crop arrives when it is ready, not when the customer wants it. It also creates a risk of wastage. Produce can be rejected because it is bruised, oddly shaped, or simply because there is more of it than the market needs that week. For a new entrepreneur, planning for unpredictable harvests and demand is essential. Crop cycles, storage and transport need to be flexible enough to handle surplus produce or unexpected delays. The more fragile the system, the more one bad season can hurt. 6. Know your numbers There is a natural temptation to think that a business built around a good cause will eventually work itself out. The co-founder has learnt otherwise. Organic farming can involve higher planning requirements, uncertain yields, wastage, packaging costs, logistics and working capital. If these numbers are ignored, even a business with the right intentions can struggle. "You cannot build a farmer-first business if the business itself is not financially sustainable," he says. That does not mean reducing farming to profit margins. It means understanding that farmers cannot be supported by a business that keeps losing money. For him, the lesson is to calculate what each sale really costs, from sourcing and packaging to transport and wastage, before deciding whether the business can grow. The goal is to find a balance where the customer gets trustworthy food, the farmer gets a fairer return, and the business remains strong enough to keep going. 7. Give it time Perhaps the biggest investment an aspiring organic farmer needs is not money. It is patience. Soil may take time to recover . Farmers may take time to trust a new method. Customers may take time to change their buying habits. And a young business may take years before its systems begin to settle. Before investing heavily, he advises testing the soil and water, understanding what was previously grown on the land. The co-founder knows this personally. His own journey began with weekend trips to Pushkar while he was still working full time. For almost four years, he travelled between his corporate job and the farm, slowly learning what it meant to grow food. A good farm needs more than good crops "Patience is not optional in this business. It is part of the model," he says. That patience is also needed when things go wrong. A farmer may have a poor harvest. A crop may not sell. A transition may take longer than expected. A customer may question the price. The temptation is to look for a shortcut. But Deepak's experience has taught him that there are very few shortcuts when you are trying to change something as fundamental as how food is grown. Deepak's journey from corporate offices to farming has given him a broader view of an organic farming business. Growing crops without synthetic pesticides and fertilisers is only part of the work. The rest is making sure farmers earn a fair return, produce reaches customers and the business can keep going. For him, Earthy Tales is an attempt to bring soil health, farmer livelihoods and consumer wellbeing together. And for anyone thinking of starting an organic farming business, the question goes beyond how much they can grow. It is whether they can build a system in which the soil, the farmer and the customer all have a reason to stay. All pictures courtesy Deepak Sabharwal.

items.titleOriginal: Want the News to Unite People? Let Them Report It
items.description: Σε πολύ λίγες εβδομάδες, η Jackie Jantzi κάθεται στις συνεδριάσεις της σχολικής επιτροπής στο Akron του Οχάιο, κρατώντας σημειώσεις στο φορητό υπολογιστή της.
