items.descriptionOriginal: E very few weeks, Jackie Jantzi sits in on school board meetings in Akron, Ohio, taking notes on her laptop. Afterward, she polishes a summary of what happened, to be published online, free for anyone to read. Jantzi is there working for local news website Signal Akron , but she isn’t a professional reporter. She’s one of hundreds of city residents deployed by the news outlet to record what happens at local government meetings, through a program called Documenters . The write-ups they produce don’t just help the news outlet cover far more than would otherwise be possible with its staff of six reporters; they also create a public record where Akronites can follow the nitty gritty of the local decisions shaping their community. “National politics feels like you have zero power, you know? It just feels so big and out of your hands,” Jantzi says. “But any sort of civic engagement, like Documenters or even getting to know your neighbors, gives you a little bit of power locally.” As thousands of local news outlets have shrunk or shuttered , many Americans have lost reliable sources of information about municipal budget negotiations and school board votes. In their stead, national news has comprised a larger share of the public’s media diet, drawing attention to partisan divides and widening political polarization. By spotlighting community level issues, local news sources are finding ways to invigorate interest around what’s happening in their communities, helping people to refocus on public decision-making in their own backyards — which tends to fall less along the national red-blue divide. A Documenter on assignment in Chicago. Credit: City Bureau “When people have a chance to be able to talk about politics with nuance, to talk about how decisions that are being made in government affect their neighborhoods and communities, it drastically changes the types of conversations that folks have about things like health care, like access to food, like immigration,” says Max Resnik, who is helping to grow a network of 25 local Documenters programs across the country. Local news has suffered for the last three decades amid competition for attention — first from cable news, then the internet and now social media, explains Johanna Dunaway, a professor of political science at Syracuse University. As revenue dropped, outlets invested less in their newsrooms, leaving diminished staff capacity to report on towns and neighborhoods. In 2002, for every 100,000 Americans, there were 40 journalists covering local news . Today, the rate works out to 7.8. In many places, entire outlets have disappeared. Almost 40 percent of local newspapers have closed since 2005, and about one in seven Americans now live in counties with only one or no source of local news. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Those closures have been shown to have a significant effect on political division. In a study assessing the relationship between newspaper closures and polarized voting, Dunaway and colleagues found that split-ticket voting — when people vote for candidates of different parties on the same ballot — decreased by a small but notable 1.9 percent in communities that had lost a newspaper before the 2012 election. A factor driving polarization, she explains, is that Americans’ attention has shifted to the national stage. “Most of the political news stories are framed in terms of the parties waging wars against each other,” says Dunaway, “whereas local news is more about the issues that face your school district, your garbage collection, the potholes, traffic — things that are less partisan in nature.” Dunaway’s study of voting patterns caught the eye of Julie Makinen, then-executive editor of the Desert Sun newspaper in southern California. Makinen launched an experiment: For a month, the opinion section ditched syndicated columns and letters about national disputes for locally authored commentaries and California-focused political cartoons. Credit: City Bureau “Local news gives people so many different touch points to connect with people in their community.” —Julie Makinen The test provided a living lab for Dunaway and her colleagues. They found that removing national politics from the opinion section didn’t reverse polarization in the Palm Springs region, but it did slow down feelings of distance between people of different political positions. The exact cause of this is unclear, according to Dunaway. Is it from increasing attention on less ideologically divided local issues? Or reducing consumption of national, more partisan news? But one of the clearest insights, she says, is that it’s viable for publications to reduce national news coverage. “People had opinions and complaints, but they, on the whole, were mostly glad to see less national stuff and more local.” For Makinen, the experience speaks to the importance of forums for civil discussion about local issues. And the community seemed to agree. When Gannett, the paper’s owner, discontinued the opinion section, community members worked with Makinen to raise money to continue to pay for an opinion editor. That fundraising effort became the Coachella Valley Journalism Foundation , a nonprofit that now supports newsrooms across the region with trainings, awards and funding for newsroom jobs. The stories local outlets cover about what’s happening at the city and county level have a much bigger impact on people’s lives than the national stage, Makinen notes. And, they create openings where community members can build relationships with each other. “Local news gives people so many different touch points to connect with people in their community, and sort of feel less isolated and polarized,” she says. Documenters is one way local news is helping community members find those touch points. The approach to citizen journalism was developed in Chicago by the nonprofit news outlet City Bureau, when the editorial team decided to recruit residents to help comb through a massive police document. It would have taken one reporter dozens of hours alone, explains Resnik. But by bringing in residents interested in flexing their research muscles, the outlet expanded its capacity and built new relationships with the community. Participants at a Documenters training session. Credit: City Bureau That evolved into Documenters, a model Resnik describes as a “civic side hustle,” where community members are paid a stipend to, as he says, “commit these small acts of journalism.” The approach has since been adopted in 25 communities, each run locally by a news or civic organization. In Ohio, Signal Akron launched three years ago simultaneously with their Documenters program, building the network of residents into the way the publication operates. Each week, community editor Kevin Dilley recruits from a pool of more than 400 trained Documenters to cover about a dozen local meetings. Documenters apply to cover meetings as fits their schedule, and make about $90 per meeting. They write up summaries, highlighting a few points they find most important. After some light editing, summaries are posted on the Documenters Akron website. If something particularly noteworthy happens, the summary may get published on Signal Akron’s main website, alongside stories written by the outlet’s professional journalists. The program, according to Dilley, has resulted in an extraordinarily diverse newsroom. Documenters range in age from 19 to 84, some with PhDs, others reentering from incarceration. Every zip code in the greater Akron area is represented. For Dilley, this community-driven approach provides an opportunity to rebuild trust in local news. Residents may be skeptical of news media, and even of Signal Akron. “Here’s the thing with the Documenters,” he says. “You trust your neighbors.” One of the biggest challenges is funding. In Akron, there are more public meetings — and more Documenters interested in covering them — than the small editorial team can handle. Dunaway, of Syracuse University, notes that there is a resurgence of attention on local news. With the internet, many anticipated that online sources about hyperlocal news issues would naturally emerge, but it didn’t happen. Now, she notes, there are concerted efforts to boost local news coverage in order to fill the need. So far, however, she says they tend to be scattershot. Urban areas tend to be better served, while rural and lower-income communities are less well-covered. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime What exactly local news looks like is also changing. Across the country, Documenters share information through messaging networks, bulletin boards and conversations with neighbors. And instead of framing local elections in the national two-party horserace, Documenters have focused on making sure community members understand the roles of the municipal positions on the ballot. “It changes this idea of an ‘us v. them’ into something where there’s much, much more nuance,” Resnik says. Jantzi believes every community should have something like a Documenters program. It’s not that local politics aren’t divisive, she says. Police issues tend to be highly polarized, and school board meetings get so contentious they stretch for hours. But by seeing meetings play out, and connecting with neighbors who are interested, there’s more awareness of the nuances of local governance. “There’s just more accountability for the decision-making and more power to the community to actually learn what’s happening,” she says. The post Want the News to Unite People? Let Them Report It appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: A scrap of patterned fabric becomes a flower petal. Another, tucked carefully into a narrow groove, forms the sleeve of a Geisha holding a lantern. Across the classroom, students lean over thermocol sheets, trimming fabric, testing colour combinations and adjusting tiny pieces until their designs begin to take shape. Students carefully tuck fabric pieces into grooves cut along their thermocol sketches, bringing designs featuring flowers, landscapes and animals to life without needles or thread. At Budha College in Karnal, Haryana, more than 100 first-year Fashion Design students spent seven hours turning discarded fabric into colourful artworks, using a Japanese art form called kinusaiga. There were no needles or threads involved. Instead, the students tucked fabric scraps into grooves cut along their sketches, creating original designs featuring flowers, landscapes, animals and abstract patterns. Guided by their teachers, Harshita Singh and Komal, the students used fabric collected on campus to explore how leftover materials could find a new purpose. Turning fabric scraps into artwork Before picking up their fabric scraps, the students began with colour theory. They explored which shades, textures and patterns worked well together before deciding what they wanted to create. Once they had settled on a design, they sketched it onto a thermocol sheet and carefully cut grooves along its outlines. Then came the task of bringing the sketches to life. From selecting colour combinations to working with intricate patterns, the seven-hour activity gave students hands-on experience with textures, design and fabric reuse. The students sorted through the discarded fabric, searching for pieces that suited their designs. Each piece had to be cut to size and pressed into the grooves, with care taken around every curve and corner. A small adjustment could change how a pattern looked or how neatly a piece of fabric fitted into place. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Budha College Learn By Doing (@budhacollege) For Reya, a first-year fashion design student from Tamil Nadu, the assignment was an opportunity to experiment with an unfamiliar art form. She chose to create a Geisha holding a lantern, using fabric collected on campus to complete the design. "By upcycling waste fabric sourced from campus into the thermocol board, I created a piece I was genuinely proud of," she says. Jahnvi, another first-year student from Jaipur, enjoyed experimenting with different colours, textures, and patterns. The exercise, she says, helped her explore art from a different perspective. Learning by doing The activity brought several aspects of fashion design together in one exercise: colour theory, an understanding of textures, material selection, and the patience needed to work with intricate details. For Harshita Singh, a faculty member in fashion design, the aim was to help students put classroom concepts into practice while giving them room to experiment with their own ideas. "As a mentor, I appreciate their patience, dedication, and creativity, because art is not just about creating something beautiful; it is about patience, passion, and enjoying the process," she says. The students' artworks, made using leftover fabric, reached a wider audience through Instagram reels that crossed 3.5 million views. The exercise also reflects Budha College's emphasis on practical learning. The skill-based institution, affiliated with Kurukshetra University, encourages students to build their abilities through assignments and projects alongside classroom instruction. According to CEO Abhinav, the broader aim is to help students become aatmanirbhar , or self-reliant, by developing practical skills they can carry forward after graduation. From a classroom assignment to millions of views The finished artworks found an audience well beyond the classroom. Reels featuring the students' creations crossed 3.5 million views on Instagram, giving the first-year students an unexpected opportunity to share their work with a much larger audience. Reshmi, a student from Bangladesh, said the activity gave the class a chance to express its creativity while working with discarded materials. Laxmi from Odisha initially found the technique difficult but said it became easier and more enjoyable with practice. The seven-hour exercise gave first-year students a chance to put their design skills to the test, turning classroom concepts into beautiful artworks. The artworks were created as part of a classroom assignment. They are not for sale and are not linked to a commercial venture or social cause. The focus was on learning a new technique, experimenting with materials, and understanding how fabric could be reused creatively. By the end of the seven-hour exercise, the students had turned leftover fabric into individual works of art, each shaped by their choices of colour, pattern, and design. And without using a single stitch, they had found another way to work with material that might otherwise have been thrown away. All images courtesy of Budha College

items.description: «Αν πέσουν 90 χιλιοστά βροχής σε δύο ώρες, οποιαδήποτε πόλη στον κόσμο θα πλημμυρίσει», λέει ο Δρ Subimal Ghosh, Πρόεδρος του Ινστιτούτου Καθηγητής στο Τμήμα Πολιτικών Μηχανικών και Συνέδριο του Διεπιστημονικού Προγράμματος για τις Κλιματικές Σπουδές στο IIT Bombay, εξηγώντας ότι καμία πόλη στον κόσμο, ανεξάρτητα από τις δημόσιες υποδομές, δεν μπορεί να αποτρέψει τις πλημμύρες.…
items.descriptionOriginal: "If 90 mm of rain occurs in two hours, any city in the world will flood," says Dr Subimal Ghosh, Institute Chair Professor in the Department of Civil Engineering and Convener of the Interdisciplinary Program in Climate Studies at IIT Bombay, explaining that no city in the world, irrespective of the public infrastructure in place, can prevent flooding at that intensity of rainfall. For instance, Mumbai receives extreme rainfall (300-500 mm) in just three to four days every monsoon. Ghosh believes the real question is no longer whether the city can stop flooding, but how quickly it can warn people before the water rises. And for that, he points to a model built 1,800 kilometres away, on India's eastern coast. A cyclone that changed everything On 29 October 1999, a super cyclone tore through Odisha with winds crossing 250 kmph, killing close to 10,000 people. It remains one of India's deadliest natural disasters. Two decades later, cyclones of comparable intensity strike the same coastline and claim a fraction of the lives once lost, largely because of a warning and evacuation system built brick by brick since that tragedy. IAS officer Pradeep Kumar Jena , who has managed disaster response in Odisha for over 20 years, has spoken about the state's "zero-human-casualty" mission, a goal set after 1999 and pursued relentlessly since. When Cyclone Fani, Odisha evacuated over a million people. When Cyclone Fani struck in 2019 with wind speeds exceeding 200 kmph, the state evacuated over a million people and limited the toll to a few dozen deaths. During Cyclone Amphan in 2020, of comparable ferocity to the 1999 storm, Odisha recorded only a handful of fatalities in the state, even as overall regional casualties stayed under 100. What the system actually looks like The Odisha State Disaster Management Authority, set up in 2000 as India's first dedicated body of its kind, anchors a layered warning network. IMD forecasts and satellite tracking feed into a chain of over 800 multipurpose cyclone shelters and watchtowers across 120-plus coastal locations, from where sirens and mass alerts reach nearly 1,200 villages down to the last mile. District collectors carry satellite phones and HAM radios so communication survives even when towers fall. A trained cadre of over 100,000 volunteers, alongside gram panchayats and women's self-help groups, runs evacuations and manages relief camps, while twice-yearly mock drills keep the machinery ready before cyclone season begins. Dr Mrutyunjay Mohapatra, Director General of the IMD and an Odisha native, has led much of the country's cyclone forecasting work behind this system, calling accurate, lead-time forecasting the single biggest lifesaver. Why forecasting made the difference Structural fixes for urban flooding require geotechnical, structural, and water engineers working together over years, and solutions cannot simply be copied from cities like those in Japan without understanding local implications, Ghosh explains. IMD forecasts and satellite tracking feed into a chain of over 800 multipurpose cyclone shelters and watchtowers across 120-plus coastal locations, from where sirens and mass alerts reach nearly 1,200 villages down to the last mile. Early warning, meanwhile, can save lives immediately. "I would rather stress that we should have a very good early warning system. This is what I always tell," he says. "With early warning, we can save a lot of people by making quick decisions," pointing to Cyclone Dana's 2024 forecast-driven school closures as an example. He calls this kind of forecasting work a silent scientific revolution, one that has quietly saved tens of thousands of lives without much public recognition. A blueprint that other states have borrowed Odisha's approach has not stayed confined to its coastline. Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, and West Bengal have built similar community-based disaster preparedness and early warning frameworks, and the World Bank-backed National Cyclone Risk Mitigation Project has extended comparable shelters, evacuation infrastructure, and warning systems across ten coastal states since 2010. A dedicated IIT Bombay–BMC working group shares real-time monsoon data. Community-based disaster preparedness manuals developed in Odisha were translated for wider circulation specifically so other states could adapt them. Researchers now regularly cite the "Odisha model" as a benchmark against which other coastal states measure their own preparedness. Mumbai's own experiment IIT Bombay has already built mumbaiflood.in, a portal offering a three-day rainfall forecast, a 90-minute radar-based nowcast, and a continuously updated flood inundation model, which received over 10,000 visits within days of launch. A dedicated IIT Bombay–BMC working group shares this data in real time, and Ghosh describes the civic body's response as prompt, citing pump operations adjusted based on the institute's forecasts. A new crowdsourced flood-reporting feature now adds ground-truth data from citizens to the model, and Ghosh believes Mumbai needs the same last-mile relay Odisha uses, since "not everyone can have access to internet, but at least a few people will have access, and they can immediately inform others." As Odisha's mangrove replanting drives show, resilience is often built through unglamorous, sustained science rather than singular fixes. Odisha's cyclone story suggests India already has a working model. The task now, experts say, is fine-tuning it for a flooding megacity. All images courtesy of TNIE Sources: ' Cyclone Biparjoy: IAS Officer Who Led Odisha's Stellar Disaster Management' : by The Better India, Published on 13 June 2023 ' Saving Over 1 Million Lives: How Odisha Saw Cyclone Fani in The Eye & Came Out Strong ': by The Better India, Published on 6 May 2019 ' Odisha's turnaround in disaster management has lessons for the world ': by The World Bank, Published on 3 November 2023 ' What states can learn from Odisha in disaster preparedness and mitigation ': by ReliefWeb/World Bank, Published on 14 June 2019 ' The "Odisha model" for disaster resilience ': by Ideas for India, Published on 16 August 2024

items.descriptionOriginal: Την ανάγκη να διασφαλιστούν οι κατάλληλες τεχνικές και επιστημονικές προϋποθέσεις για την εφαρμογή του Ψηφιακού Αποθετηρίου Διαγνωστικών Εξετάσεων αναδεικνύει ο Ιατρικός Σύλλογος Πειραιώς (ΙΣΠ), προειδοποιώντας για τις δυσκολίες που ενδέχεται να αντιμετωπίσουν τα διαγνωστικά εργαστήρια κατά τη μετάβαση στο νέο σύστημα. Σε ανακοίνωσή του, ο Σύλλογος τονίζει ότι ο ψηφιακός εκσυγχρονισμός της Υγείας είναι αναγκαίος, επισημαίνει ωστόσο πως η εφαρμογή του πρέπει να συνοδεύεται από σαφείς προδιαγραφές, επαρκή τεχνική υποστήριξη και εύλογο χρόνο προσαρμογής, ώστε να μην επηρεαστούν η λειτουργία των εργαστηρίων και η αποζημίωση των παρεχόμενων υπηρεσιών. Οι επισημάνσεις του ΙΣΠ ακολουθούν συνάντηση με τη συμμετοχή εκπροσώπων της ΗΔΥΚΑ, του ΕΟΠΥΥ, του ΚΕΤΕΚΝΥ, της ΠΟΣΙΠΥ, του ΠΑΣΙΔΙΚ και της ΕΣΠΥ, κατά την οποία εξετάστηκαν οι προκλήσεις που συνδέονται με την ηλεκτρονική καταχώρηση των αποτελεσμάτων και την αντιστοίχιση των διαγνωστικών εξετάσεων με τους διεθνείς κωδικούς LOINC. Τα ζητήματα που θέτει ο Ιατρικός Σύλλογος Πειραιώς Σύμφωνα με όσα αναφέρει ο ΙΣΠ, η καταχώρηση των αποτελεσμάτων στο Ψηφιακό Αποθετήριο αποτελεί άμεση προτεραιότητα για τα εργαστήρια, καθώς η μη συμμόρφωση με τις προβλεπόμενες διαδικασίες ενδέχεται να επηρεάσει την αποζημίωσή τους. Ιδιαίτερη έμφαση δίνεται στην εφαρμογή του συστήματος κωδικοποίησης LOINC, το οποίο χρησιμοποιείται για την τυποποιημένη αναγνώριση εργαστηριακών εξετάσεων και άλλων κλινικών παρατηρήσεων. Όπως επισημαίνει ο Σύλλογος, η σωστή αντιστοίχιση δεν αποτελεί μια απλή διαδικασία καταχώρησης κωδικών. Προϋποθέτει την ακριβή αποτύπωση επιστημονικών παραμέτρων, όπως η μέθοδος της εξέτασης, το είδος του δείγματος και οι μονάδες μέτρησης. Κατά τον ΙΣΠ, η πολυπλοκότητα αυτής της διαδικασίας καθιστά προβληματική την εφαρμογή ασφυκτικών χρονοδιαγραμμάτων, ιδιαίτερα όταν οι εργαστηριακοί γιατροί καλούνται να αναλάβουν την ευθύνη ελέγχου χιλιάδων κωδικών χωρίς πλήρη τεκμηρίωση και κατάλληλη τεχνική υποστήριξη. Πρόταση για διεπιστημονική επιτροπή Για την αντιμετώπιση των παραπάνω ζητημάτων, ο Ιατρικός Σύλλογος Πειραιώς ζητά τη συγκρότηση διεπιστημονικής επιτροπής, με τη συμμετοχή των αρμόδιων δημόσιων φορέων, εργαστηριακών γιατρών, εταιρειών πληροφορικής και κατασκευαστών ιατρικού εξοπλισμού. Σύμφωνα με την πρότασή του, η επιτροπή θα πρέπει να αναλάβει τον επιστημονικό έλεγχο των αντιστοιχίσεων, να συμβάλει στην πιλοτική εφαρμογή του συστήματος και να διασφαλίσει επαρκή μεταβατική περίοδο πριν από την επιβολή οικονομικών κυρώσεων. Βασικό αίτημα του Συλλόγου είναι να μη συνδεθεί η αποζημίωση των εργαστηριακών εξετάσεων με διαδικασίες που, όπως υποστηρίζει, δεν έχουν ακόμη ολοκληρωθεί και δοκιμαστεί επαρκώς. Ν. Πλατανησιώτης: «Αναγκαία η τεχνική ετοιμότητα και η εύλογη μεταβατική περίοδος» Αναφερόμενος στο ζήτημα, ο πρόεδρος του Ιατρικού Συλλόγου Πειραιώς, Νικόλαος Πλατανησιώτης, υπογράμμισε ότι η ψηφιακή αναβάθμιση των υπηρεσιών Υγείας πρέπει να προχωρήσει με τη συνεργασία των επαγγελματιών που καλούνται να εφαρμόσουν τις νέες διαδικασίες. «Ο ψηφιακός εκσυγχρονισμός της Υγείας είναι αναγκαίος, αλλά πρέπει να εφαρμόζεται με επιστημονική τεκμηρίωση, τεχνική επάρκεια και ουσιαστική συνεργασία με τους γιατρούς. Δεν είναι αποδεκτό να συνδέεται η αποζημίωση μιας εξέτασης με διαδικασίες που δεν έχουν ολοκληρωθεί και δοκιμαστεί επαρκώς» , δήλωσε. Ο κ. Πλατανησιώτης ζήτησε σαφείς προδιαγραφές, ουσιαστική συμμετοχή των εργαστηριακών γιατρών και επαρκή χρόνο προσαρμογής, προκειμένου το σύστημα να λειτουργήσει αποτελεσματικά προς όφελος τόσο των επαγγελματιών Υγείας όσο και των ασθενών. Συνοψίζοντας τη θέση του Συλλόγου, υπογράμμισε ότι η επιτυχία της νέας διαδικασίας προϋποθέτει τρία βασικά στοιχεία: «Τεχνική ετοιμότητα, επιστημονικό έλεγχο και εύλογη μεταβατική περίοδο». Ειδήσεις σήμερα Μπορεί μια απλή φωτογραφία προσώπου να αποκαλύψει πόσο άρρωστοι είμαστε; Τι είναι η ΧΑΠ από την οποία πάσχει ο Βασίλης Παπακωνσταντίνου, ποια τα συμπτώματα και πώς αντιμετωπίζεται Η Ελληνική Διαβητολογική Εταιρεία τιμά τον κ. items.descriptionOriginal: A powerful new AI system could help doctors detect pancreatic cancer years before it becomes visible on conventional scans. The technology, called REDMOD, identified hidden warning signs an average of 475 days before diagnosis and was nearly twice as sensitive as experienced radiologists. By spotting cancer-related changes at their earliest stages, it could dramatically improve the chances of successful treatment for one of the deadliest forms of cancer.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Burrowing Owls Nesting on Solar Farms are Rewriting a Species’ Future Reading Time: 3 minutes Burrowing owls nesting on solar farms are showing that clean energy and wildlife habitat can share the same land. Burrowing owls nesting on solar farms are turning a renewable energy site into an unlikely nursery. More than a dozen owlets hatched this summer inside plastic tunnels at a 10,000-acre solar complex near Phoenix, Arizona. The project suggests clean energy and vulnerable wildlife can thrive side by side. Longroad Energy, the solar company that runs the site, teamed up with Wild at Heart , a raptor rehabilitation center. Together they set out to test whether burrowing owls nesting on solar farms could raise families long-term. In March, workers moved nine owl pairs and one single male about 50 miles to the site, since their old burrows were about to be destroyed by new housing. Burrowing owls are small, ground-dwelling birds of prey roughly the size of a loaf of bread, perched on long, stilt-like legs. They typically nest in tunnels dug by animals like ground squirrels and prairie dogs. Since the 1960s, their numbers have dropped by more than a third across the United States. Housing and farmland development keep shrinking that habitat. Conservation groups often relocate colonies before bulldozers arrive, moving them to farmland where they can hunt. But as farmland gets bought up too, safe new sites are harder to find. The Wild at Heart’s Burrowing Owl team had nearly run out of nearby options. They used to drive displaced owls about 50 miles to open farmland. Now some trips stretch 60 to 100 miles, which is too costly to sustain, even though the owls need very little space to settle in. Solar farms offered a new possibility for relocation. Utility-scale solar energy, meaning large power plants built to serve the electric grid, has expanded quickly across Arizona. That growth can squeeze desert wildlife, but it also helps slow climate change, a threat already putting many U.S. bird species at risk. State law required Longroad to survey wildlife before building its Sun Streams project. That survey found eight burrowing owls already living on the land. The discovery connected the company with Wild at Heart, which was running low on relocation space, sparking a larger experiment in burrowing owls nesting on solar farms. Burrowing owls nesting on solar farms emerged as a conservation solution when Longroad Energy’s pre-construction wildlife survey found eight owls already living on the land, connecting the company with Wild at Heart at a moment when the raptor center was running out of relocation space for displaced desert birds. Photo by Greg Clark courtesy of Wild at Heart . After construction finished, Longroad offered Wild at Heart around 250 acres between two Sun Streams projects. Workers installed 40 artificial burrows and placed a breeding pair in each, at first surrounded by netting so the birds would not fly back home. They also set up lights to attract insects and delivered mice daily while the owls adjusted. The company funded feeding and monitoring through the entire breeding season, support Wild at Heart normally cannot afford beyond 30 days. Within one month, every female had laid eggs, an early sign that burrowing owls nesting on solar farms might actually work. By late June, 36 chicks had hatched. Within three months, 29 young owls had fledged and left the nest, and staff slowly stopped feeding them so the birds would learn to hunt on their own. The team began spotting insect remains in their droppings, an encouraging sign. By the end of August, Wild at Heart stopped feedings altogether. Researchers are now studying how to expand this kind of coexistence. A 2025 Arizona State University study found that prime solar sites overlap with burrowing owl habitat by about 13% across seven Western states. The nonprofit Renewable Energy Wildlife Institute is building a database to help solar companies weigh biodiversity when choosing where to build. Arizona is also drafting guidelines to help future solar projects support wildlife instead of displacing it. Wild at Heart hopes to grow vegetation on solar sites to attract insects and rodents for owls to eat, turning relocation sites into lasting habitat. Longroad is even discussing solar panel designs that could capture water from humid air to help plants grow nearby. Small changes like that could make future sites more welcoming for burrowing owls nesting on solar farms from day one. The raptor conservation group hopes to bring more solar companies on board. Burrowing owls nesting on solar farms may soon become less of an experiment and more of a model other developers can copy. If more companies adopt the practice, displaced owl colonies could find lasting homes on the very land built to power their neighbors. For a bird that has lost so much ground, that shift offers a real reason for hope. The post How Burrowing Owls Nesting on Solar Farms are Rewriting a Species’ Future appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: 1 Plant, 100 Uses explores the many ways familiar Indian plants, leaves, fruits and trees have been part of everyday life — from food and farming to homes, traditions and natural remedies. Each story takes one plant and uncovers the surprising ways people have found it useful, often across generations. In many Indian homes, the banana plant is a familiar sight . People buy its fruit at local markets, and they use its leaves during festivals and family gatherings. But the plant has uses that go well beyond what most people see in their kitchens. Farmers and artisans have found ways to use parts usually left behind after harvest. Some have been part of Indian food traditions for generations, while others are helping turn farm waste into useful products. Here are a few ways the banana plant is used across India. 1. Ripe bananas make an easy snack Bananas are eaten across India as a snack or alongside breakfast. They are easy to carry and can be eaten without cooking once ripe. Farmers and artisans have found ways to use parts usually left behind after harvest. Photograph: (Image generated by AI) The fruit is also used to make products that last longer than fresh bananas. The ICAR National Research Centre for Banana documents the processing of bananas into products such as juice and banana fig. Banana pulp can also be used in jams and other preparations. 2. Raw bananas are a kitchen staple Raw bananas are cooked in homes across India. They are added to curries and dry vegetable dishes and are used in fried snacks. In Kerala, raw bananas are used to make the much-loved banana chips. The Nendran variety is particularly popular for this purpose. Raw bananas can also be dried and milled into flour for use in different food products. The Indian Council of Agricultural Research has documented ways to process bananas into products with a longer shelf life. Such methods can help reduce losses when fresh produce cannot be sold or consumed in time. 3. The banana flower is cooked as a vegetable The purple flower that hangs beneath a bunch of bananas is used in several regional cuisines. Once the outer bracts are removed, the small florets can be cleaned and cooked in curries and stir-fries. Banana flower dishes are found in parts of southern and eastern India. The flower can also be made into pickles. The ICAR National Research Centre for Banana has documented banana flower pickle as a value-added product. Preparing the flower takes time because the florets need to be cleaned individually. But in households where it is a familiar ingredient, this is normally part of cooking with the plant. 4. The tender inner stem is eaten The part commonly called the banana stem is actually a pseudostem made up of tightly packed leaf sheaths. At its centre is a tender core that is used in cooking. In many Indian homes, the banana plant is a familiar sight. Photograph: (Image generated by AI) In southern Indian kitchens, the core is chopped and cooked as a vegetable. It is also used in juices and other preparations. The ICAR National Research Centre for Banana has documented products such as candy and pickles made from the central core. Using the inner core for food gives households another way to make use of the plant after its fruit has been harvested. 5. Banana leaves are used to serve food A meal served on a banana leaf is a familiar sight in many parts of southern India. The broad leaf holds rice and several accompaniments and is widely used during weddings and festivals. Banana leaves are also used to wrap certain foods and serve meals at community gatherings. Their size makes them convenient for serving a complete meal on one surface. The leaves have a place in traditional food practices as well as in everyday hospitality. Their use varies by region and occasion. 6. The pseudostem is turned into fibre After the banana bunch is harvested, the pseudostem is cut down. Instead of leaving all this material unused, farmers and entrepreneurs can process it to extract natural fibre. The Indian Council of Agricultural Research has documented banana fibre processing technology and its transfer to an entrepreneur in Uttar Pradesh. The fibre can be used to make ropes and garments as well as mats and carpets. Bags and baskets are other possible products. Processing the pseudostem requires equipment and suitable facilities. Where these are available, the material can become a source of raw material for small businesses. 7. Banana fibre is used in handicrafts The fibre extracted from banana plant material can be used to make items such as table mats and cushion covers. These products offer another use for material left behind after harvesting. In January 2024, the ICAR National Research Centre for Banana organised a training programme in Tamil Nadu on banana fibre craft and value addition. The programme aimed to help women learn skills that could be used to make products from banana sheath and its by-products. The ICAR report on the programme describes the initiative and its focus on developing craft skills. For those with access to training and buyers, such work can provide an additional source of income. In Kerala, raw bananas are used to make the much-loved banana chips. Photograph: (PlotMyGarden) 8. Banana peels need not go straight into the bin Banana peels are usually discarded once the fruit has been eaten. Yet they can be put to use in food processing and composting. The ICAR National Research Centre for Banana has documented banana peel pickle as one way of using this part of the fruit. At home, the peels can be chopped and added to a compost bin along with other kitchen scraps and dry material. As the organic matter breaks down, it becomes part of the compost. This is a practical option for households that grow plants or maintain a garden. 9. Banana plants are used during ceremonies Banana plants are commonly used to decorate entrances and ceremonial spaces during weddings and religious occasions in several parts of India. Their green leaves and upright pseudostems are a familiar part of these arrangements. The plant is associated with auspicious occasions in many communities. The exact customs differ across regions, but banana plants continue to feature in traditional celebrations . Their role during these occasions is distinct from their use as food or raw material. They are part of the way families mark important events. 10. Banana residue can be used on farms Harvesting bananas leaves behind considerable plant material. The pseudostem and other suitable residues can be considered for composting or other forms of farm use rather than being discarded without thought. Research published through the Indian Council of Agricultural Research discusses banana plant parts and their place in integrated farming systems. The best use depends on the farm and the resources available. Some growers may be able to supply material to fibre processors while others may find composting more practical. The fibre extracted from banana plant material can be used to make items such as table mats and cushion covers. Photograph: (Bunnings) Making use of what remains The banana plant serves different purposes in different parts of India. Its fruit and flower are cooked in homes while its leaves are used for serving food. These uses also offer farmers and small businesses ways to get more value from a crop . With suitable processing and local demand, parts of the plant that are left behind can become useful materials.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News The Comoros Turns Climate Ambition into Action with a Plan Focused on Forests, Water, and Geothermal Energy Reading Time: 3 minutes Despite producing almost no greenhouse gas emissions, the Comoros is turning climate ambition into action through a $6.6 billion national plan backed by forest restoration, water security projects, and a new geothermal power plant. Turning climate ambition into action is now central to how the Union of Comoros plans its future . This volcanic archipelago on the Southeastern African side of the Indian Ocean produces almost no greenhouse gas emissions of its own. Yet it faces some of the world’s most severe climate risks. The country is also a global biodiversity hotspot, home to unique forests and coral reefs. Roughly a fifth of the population already lives in poverty, with another fifth at risk. Cyclones and droughts threaten to push even more families into hardship each year. In the last decade, two major cyclones have struck the islands hard. Cyclone Kenneth affected 40% of the population in 2019. Cyclone Chido followed in 2024, again damaging homes, crops, and infrastructure. In March 2026, the Comoros submitted an updated climate plan to the United Nations. The plan, called a Nationally Determined Contribution, or NDC, sets ambitious new targets. It aims to cut emissions by 14 to 57 percent by 2035, depending on outside support. Full implementation of the plan is expected to cost about $6.6 billion by 2030. The UN Development Programme (UNDP), is helping the country secure that funding. Early support has already unlocked millions of dollars from international climate funds. Adaptation sits at the heart of the country’s climate strategy. The Comoros plans to reforest 8,000 hectares of land over the coming years. It also aims to restore 1,000 hectares of mangroves and 600 hectares of coral reefs. Agriculture depends heavily on a healthy environment across the islands. Export crops like vanilla, ylang-ylang, and cloves support many rural livelihoods. Protecting these value chains from climate shocks is now a funding priority for UNDP and its partners. Forest and mangrove restoration could bring added financial benefits over time. The Comoros is exploring carbon credit markets under the Paris Agreement’s Article 6. Its forestry and mangrove sectors may become key assets for future carbon projects. Water security remains an urgent challenge across the islands. Grande Comore has no permanent rivers and relies mainly on rainfall. The government plans to build 50 micro-dams and restore 6,000 hectares of watersheds. UNDP has already helped install climate-resilient water infrastructure in more than 50 communities. This work now serves more than 230,000 people across the islands. Local residents help maintain the boreholes, treatment plants, and reservoirs themselves. Turning climate ambition into action in the Comoros means building on UNDP’s climate-resilient water infrastructure already serving more than 230,000 people across the islands through community-maintained boreholes, treatment plants, and reservoirs. Photo courtesy of UNDP . Energy remains one of the country’s biggest sources of emissions. Diesel generators currently supply much of the electricity used in Comorian homes. Turning climate ambition into action here means building a cleaner power grid. A geothermal power plant near the Karthala volcano could help change that. Geoscience surveys have confirmed strong potential for high-temperature energy there. The project is now moving through exploration and risk-reduction studies. Planners expect the plant to generate around 15 megawatts once complete. Funding partners include the African Development Bank and the Global Environment Facility. Italy is also funding technical support to help make the project attractive to future investors. Smaller renewable projects are also expanding access to clean power. UNDP is testing solar minigrids on three separate islands. Each design includes ways for women and young people to take part. Disaster preparedness is another growing focus for the country. New data tools helped teams respond faster after Cyclone Chido struck in 2024. The government is also developing new insurance products for vulnerable communities. A national disaster risk reduction strategy now guides these efforts through 2030. The plan has already helped attract financing from the World Bank and the African Development Bank. Turning climate ambition into action increasingly means matching local plans with international partners. The full strategy appears in the country’s official Nationally Determined Contribution, filed with the United Nations. The plan also includes a social inclusion focus on women, youth, and vulnerable groups for the first time. Electricity access in the Comoros has grown from 46% in 2017 to 71% today. Each new project adds another piece to the country’s climate plan. Turning climate ambition into action, piece by piece, may be this island nation’s clearest path forward. The post The Comoros Turns Climate Ambition into Action with a Plan Focused on Forests, Water, and Geothermal Energy appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: What happens when young people see a problem that others have learned to overlook? Across the United States, a growing network of students is rescuing millions of dollars' worth of perfectly usable medical supplies destined for landfills and delivering them to communities in need. When 16-year-old Ben Kurian discovered that hospitals routinely discarded sterile supplies simply because they were nearing expiration, he began organizing donations from his kitchen table. His efforts have since grown into a movement alongside student-led organizations like Blueprints for Pangea and United2Heal, whose volunteers are redirecting medical supplies to underserved clinics around the world. Balancing schoolwork with warehouse shifts and deliveries, these young changemakers are proving that compassion, resourcefulness, and a willingness to act can make an extraordinary difference. They didn't wait for someone else to solve the problem. They simply saw a need and got to work.

items.descriptionOriginal: Few flowers can brighten a home garden like marigolds. Their cheerful yellow and orange blooms bring colour to balconies, terraces, and window ledges. They are also a familiar sight during Indian festivals, when they find their way into garlands and decorations. Growing them at home does not require a large garden, but it helps to understand what these flowers need to survive. From choosing the right variety to guaranteeing proper drainage, some useful lessons can be learnt from a farmer who has spent years cultivating marigolds. October and November are good months to grow marigolds in many parts of India, as the cooler weather can support their growth and flowering. If you are planning to add these cheerful blooms to your home garden, this is a good time to get started. Arup Kumar Ghosh, a farmer from Kolaghat in West Bengal's East Midnapore district, began his journey in floriculture in 2011. After working at a flower shop in Hyderabad, he returned to his hometown and decided to cultivate marigolds himself. His first attempt was not successful. The local saplings he bought produced small flowers that did not meet market standards, resulting in losses. Determined to improve their quality, he travelled to Thailand and spent six months training at the Bangkok Blossom Market. There, he learnt about the Tennis Ball marigold variety, prized for its bright, round flowers. He brought back seeds of the yellow and orange varieties and began cultivating them on leased land. Reflecting on his early experiments, he told The Better India, "In the early stages of farming, I had to experiment with different fertilisers and treatments to find what worked best. It was all trial and error." Over time, he developed his cultivation practices and expanded his farm. His experience offers several useful lessons for anyone looking to grow marigolds at home. 1. Give your marigolds plenty of sunlight Sunlight is one of the first things to consider when deciding where to grow marigolds. A shaded corner may not be the best place for these flowering plants. October and November are good months to grow marigolds in many parts of India. Arup explains, "Marigolds need plenty of sunlight, so I make sure the land is not overshadowed by tall trees or other obstacles." For home gardeners, this means choosing a sunny spot on a balcony, terrace, or in the garden. Place your pots where the plants can receive several hours of direct sunlight each day. If possible, avoid locations where taller plants or walls block the light for most of the day. 2. Choose your seeds and variety carefully Arup learnt the importance of choosing the right planting material through experience. The local marigold saplings he initially purchased produced small flowers that were not suitable for his business. During his training in Thailand, he discovered a new variety. He explains, "I learnt about a high-quality flower called the Tennis Ball marigold variety. This is prized for its bright, round flowers and its ability to withstand long-distance shipping without being damaged." For a home garden, you can choose marigold seeds or saplings from a reliable nursery. Consider the space available, the colour you prefer, and the size of the flowers you want to grow. If you are new to gardening, starting with healthy saplings may be easier than raising plants from seeds. Check the leaves and stems before buying them, and avoid plants that appear diseased or badly damaged. 3. Make sure the soil drains well Water management has been an important part of Arup's farming experience, particularly during the monsoon. "The key is ensuring the fields don't retain too much water, especially during the monsoon," he says. "I have to ensure the drainage system is effective, so the water doesn't stagnate and harm the plants." The same principle applies to marigolds grown in pots. Choose containers with drainage holes and use a potting mix that allows excess water to escape. Do not leave pots standing in water collected in trays. Pests can affect flowering plants in home gardens as well as commercial farms. Photograph: (Bishy Barnabee's) Check the soil before watering. If it is still moist, wait before adding more water. The aim is to provide enough moisture for healthy growth without leaving the roots sitting in waterlogged soil. 4. Keep an eye out for pests Pests can affect flowering plants in home gardens as well as commercial farms. Regularly checking your marigolds can help you spot problems before they spread. The farmer shares his approach to managing pests, saying, "Instead of relying on harmful chemicals, I use neem oil, bone dust, and cow dung manure." For home gardeners, it is important to understand that these materials serve different purposes. Neem oil products may help manage certain pests when used according to the label instructions. Bone dust and cow dung manure are soil amendments, not direct substitutes for pest control. Inspect the leaves and stems regularly for insects or unusual changes. If you use manure, make sure it is well-rotted and suitable for gardening. Use any fertiliser or soil amendment in the recommended quantity. 5. Take precautions during heavy rain Unpredictable weather can damage marigold crops, particularly when heavy rain causes water to collect around the roots. Arup explains, "I cover the field with a net so they can grow well during harsh weather conditions." A home garden will have different needs from a commercial farm, but a few easy precautions can still help. Move small pots to a sheltered area when strong winds or heavy rain are forecast. Secure taller plants so that they do not topple over, and make sure the drainage holes remain clear. Sunlight is one of the first things to consider when deciding where to grow marigolds. Photograph: (Gardening Know How) After heavy rain, check your pots for standing water and allow excess moisture to drain away. 6. Be patient and learn from experience The farmer's journey was not without setbacks. His first crop did not produce the quality he wanted, and he had to experiment with different methods before finding what worked for him. Home gardeners can take a similar approach by observing their plants and making adjustments when necessary. If your marigolds are not healthy, check whether they receive enough sunlight, whether the soil drains properly, and whether there are signs of pests. Use a fertiliser suitable for flowering plants and follow the recommended dosage. Avoid making several changes at once, as this can make it harder to understand what is helping or harming the plant. Arup learnt the importance of choosing the right planting material through experience. Photograph: (Flowers Guide) Growing marigolds at home Arup Kumar Ghosh's experience shows how observation, experimentation, and patience can help improve marigold cultivation. While growing flowers in a few pots is different from managing a commercial farm, the basics remain relevant. With the right growing conditions and consistent care, marigolds can bring a welcome splash of colour to your home garden. TBI Gardening Calendar brings together what to plant, grow, and care for each month of the year, helping home gardeners make the most of their balconies, terraces, backyards, and small growing spaces. Each story focuses on seasonal plants and crops, with simple, practical guidance on when to sow or plant, how to care for them, and what to expect as they grow.

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM If you’ve ever moved a bit of food off your own plate just so your dog could eat, too, then you know the feeling this program is trying to address. It’s a pretty common one in New York City right now. And most people who surrender a pet to a shelter aren’t doing it lightly. They do it as the very last resort, when they’ve truly run out of ways to make it work. NYC has put $500,000 toward the problem. The city is funding 22 food pantries across all five boroughs to stock and distribute free pet food, with supplies expected to start arriving within about two weeks. Teddy and everyone like him Cassandra, a Brooklyn resident, has a three-year-old Shih Tzu named Teddy, who she’s had since he was two months old. “Sometimes I have to sacrifice a little of my food that way he doesn’t go hungry, until I can get more food for him,” she said. At The Campaign Against Hunger in Brooklyn, pantry director Tamara Dawson has watched the same dynamic for years. “They bring their pets with them and are feeding them online because they have been without,” she said. The organization already offers free pet food to clients, but the supply has always depended on chasing grants and donors. The city funding makes that a little less precarious. What happened after SNAP cuts St. John’s Bread and Life in Brooklyn received a $17,000 voucher through the initiative. Staff said demand has grown since many clients saw their SNAP benefits reduced, something that moved through the whole household budget , pets included. “The affordability crisis affects every member of a family, including the pets we love,” said Mayor Zohran Mamdani. “No New Yorker should have to choose between feeding themselves and feeding their pets.” Animal welfare groups have tracked the connection between financial hardship and shelter surrender for years. Getting pet food to families early is a pretty practical way to keep that from happening. Where to find free pet food in NYC Here are all 22 participating locations: Bronx – Part of the Solution: 2759 Webster Ave., 10458 – New York Common Pantry: 1290 Hoe Ave., 10459 – Davidson Community Center: 2038 Davidson Ave., 10453 – The Kingsbridge Heights Community Center: 3067 Kingsbridge Terrace, 10463 Queens – First United Methodist Church of Jamaica: 162-10 Highland Ave., 11432 – River Fund: 89-11 Lefferts Boulevard, 11418 – Yeshua Worldwide Ministries Food Pantry: 7911 Caldwell Ave., 11379 – Hour Children Community Outreach: 36-49 11th Street, 11106 Brooklyn – Community Help in Park Slope: 200 Fourth Ave., 11217 – Metropolitan Council on Jewish Poverty: 5361 Preston Court, 11234 – On the Go Relief: 2832 Fulton Street, 11207 – St. John’s Bread and Life Food Pantry: 795 Lexington Ave., 11221 – The Campaign Against Hunger: 2004 Fulton Street, 11233 – YMCA Community Market: 2980 West 29th Street, 11224 Manhattan – Holy Apostles Soup Kitchen Pantry: 296 Ninth Ave., 10001 – New York Common Pantry: 8 East 109th Street, 10029 – St. Clemens Food Pantry: 423 West 46th Street, 10036 – The Father’s Heart Ministries: 543-545 East 11th Street, 10009 – The Lower Eastside Girls Club: 402 East 8th Street, 10009 – Trinity’s Services and Food for the Homeless: 602 East 9th Street, 10009 Staten Island – Project Hospitality: 205 Canal Street, 10304 – Feeding with TLC: 309 St. Paul’s Ave., 10304 Call ahead if you’re not sure what to bring or whether your nearest location is stocked yet. And if someone you know could use this, it’s the kind of thing that’s good to pass along. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Halloween might be the one night a year when the whole family ends up outside together, moving through the neighborhood in the dark. Whether that ends in magic or meltdown depends almost entirely on whether the experience matches the kid you brought with you. Dr. Kristen Cook , a board-certified pediatrician with more than 15 years of practice in the Midwest, writes that across every age, Halloween offers genuine opportunities to practice life skills like facing fears, managing expectations, developing independence, and showing kindness. How much kids are able to glean out spooky season depends on how you set it up. Toddlers and preschoolers: small excursion, low stimulation The tricky thing about Halloween for little kids is that everything exciting about it is also a lot. Unfamiliar noises, scary decorations , a neighborhood full of costumed kids running in every direction; it can tip from exciting to overwhelming fast. Dr. Cook’s rule for this age: comfortable over elaborate. Costumes shouldn’t restrict movement or vision, and there’s no reason to push through the full neighborhood circuit after dark. An early start, before it gets busy, tends to go better. Bring a wagon or stroller even if your toddler insists they don’t need one because, let’s face it, they probably will. Inspect every piece of candy before it’s touched, check for choking hazards and allergens, and agree on a daily candy limit in advance so it’s not a negotiation every time. And if the evening tips into over-stimulation, head home. A short, good Halloween beats a long, tearful one. School-age kids: independence with eyes on Elementary-age kids are ready for more. They can choose their own costumes, help decorate the house, pick out pumpkins , and have real opinions about the trick-or-treating route. Dr. Cook recommends mapping that route together in advance and letting kids take the lead once you’re out. That said, supervision doesn’t disappear. Pumpkin carving is still an adult activity at this age, and a parent or trusted adult should remain part of the outing, even if they’re hanging back a house or two. Night-friendly costume details matter more here. Think glow bracelets, LED accessories, and reflective elements. The shift at this stage is toward earned independence. Let them decide who they trick-or-treat with. Let them handle their own candy negotiations. Keep the safety guardrails in place, but make room for them to feel the difference. Teenagers: expectations and exit plans By the teenage years, Halloween looks different. Some teens feel too old for trick-or-treating; others still want to be part of it. Dr. Cook’s take is not to push them out of it. Teenagers who help hand out candy, look after younger siblings, or supervise part of the evening have a real role that doesn’t require a costume. If they’re going out independently, the conversations to have are about curfew, approved locations, and what to do if they end up somewhere uncomfortable. Dr. Cook specifically recommends creating an exit plan before they leave, so they have a way out of an uncomfortable situation without needing to explain themselves in the moment. A standing offer of a no-questions pickup goes a long way. The bigger ask for teenagers is respect. Taking more than a reasonable amount from an unattended candy bowl, or pulling pranks that leave families upset, isn’t harmless fun. Dr. Cook frames this as a chance to practice the kind of independence that looks like actual maturity. What all ages have in common The memories that stick, Dr. Cook writes, usually aren’t about the costumes or the candy. They’re about the feelings that are attached to them. They remember feeling included, connected, part of something. Halloween doesn’t require expensive gear or elaborate setups. It requires showing up for the kid in front of you, at whatever stage they’re at. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: The Sydney Opera House, with its bold, innovative architecture, is said to be one of the world’s most photographed buildings — and it may soon share that status with another venue of its kind. Opening last week along China’s Huangpu River, the Shanghai Grand Opera House truly lives up to the adjective in its title. At nearly 1.6 million square feet, the performing arts center has three auditoriums seating 4,200 guests in total and will showcase everything from baroque opera and classical music to experimental productions. But what is perhaps its most awe-worthy attraction lies not within its walls but outside them: a stunning, spiral staircase that appears to be almost suspended in air. Yumeng Zhu The staircase connects the ground level to a rooftop observation deck that also serves as a stage, and visitors can access it regardless of whether they’re attending a show (cue the onslaught of social media selfies). Yumeng Zhu Restaurants, galleries, educational facilities, and other public spaces in and around the building are designed to welcome residents and tourists alike, positioning the opera house as a cultural landmark more than merely a ticketed institution. View this post on Instagram “People should be able to enjoy the building without attending a performance. It should become part of everyday life, a place to spend time, meet others, and experience the city,” Kjetil Thorsen, co-founder of Norway-based firm Snøhetta, which designed the building, told Dezeen. “A successful landmark is not only recognized by visitors, it is also embraced by the people who live around it and make it part of their everyday lives.” Snøhetta’s proposal won an international competition in 2016, and the firm teamed up with East China Architectural Design & Research Institute, Theatre Projects, and Nagata Acoustics in 2019 to bring the project from concept to completion. Wang Xiang—Xinhua/Getty Images The 2,000-seat main auditorium, called Harmony Hall, has five levels and three balconies. Soar Theatre, with a capacity of 1,200, is intended for more intimate productions, like operettas and plays, while the third auditorium, dubbed Open Stage, seats 1,000 and features adaptable stage and seating configurations, making it ideal for experimental works. The theme of movement was intentionally woven into the building’s architecture and aesthetic, a nod to the flowing river it sits adjacent to and the bustling city in which it’s located. Large glass windows let ample light in during the day and shift the mood for visitors as the sun sets or the weather changes. Tall outdoor towers are illuminated at night, marking the venue’s place within Shanghai’s skyline. Yumeng Zhu “A cultural building, any building for that matter, must respond to its surroundings, the people who use it, the performers it serves, and the city it becomes part of,” Thorsen told Dezeen. “When I last visited the site, I was asked by a Chinese architecture student how we managed to create a building that felt so Chinese despite not being from China. The answer lies in observation and understanding context.” RELATED: “First of Its Kind”: World’s Longest Outdoor Escalator Opens in China — Take a Virtual Ride

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Testing SEHMUA Infrared Solar Wildlife and Security Cameras Reading Time: 3 minutes The SEHMUA infrared solar wildlife and security camera pairs clean solar charging with invisible night vision to observe wildlife without disruption. The home security company SEHMUA recently sent Happy Eco News a two-pack of its 2K Solar Security Cameras Wireless Outdoor for review. My recent move to a rural property provided the ideal setting to test this sponsored package. SEHMUA offered me these cameras as a home security measure, but I live in a really safe area. Property crime is not really an issue here. I said yes because rather than record human intruders, my goal is to observe local wildlife cleanly, without running invasive power cords across the land. Living alongside nature means sharing boundary land with raccoons, black-tailed deer, and, a couple of times a month, mountain lions (cougars), as neighbors report. Using an infrared solar wildlife and security camera offers an easy way to secure my property while observing wildlife and other animals that may visit when I am not home. The SEHMUA IR night vision security cameras work for wildlife too. Licensed under the Unsplash+ License Each unit pairs with a detachable solar panel and an internal rechargeable battery. Sunlight powers the hardware continuously through daylight hours. As a result, users never need to haul heavy extension cords outside or take the gear down to recharge. Hardware setup takes about five minutes per unit on an exterior wall, tree post, or fence line. The wire-free design eliminates the need to drill through exterior frames or hire an electrician. The camera delivers 2K high-definition video. A 2K image contains double the clarity of standard 1080p high definition. This sharp resolution lets property owners verify distinct coat markings, antler points, or paw prints across the perimeter. A motorized lens rotates 355 degrees horizontally and tilts 90 degrees vertically to create a 360-degree panoramic view. One device can follow a foraging raccoon across a fence line that normally requires several fixed lenses. Each unit relies on a Passive Infrared sensor, known as a PIR sensor. A PIR sensor detects living body heat rather than blowing grass or swaying tree limbs. This heat-detection focus cuts out nuisance phone alerts while ensuring deer or cougars trigger instant recordings. The unit includes 500-lumen white spotlights and an intruder alarm for standard security deterrence. Obviously, when monitoring wildlife, sudden white light can startle shy animals and disrupt natural foraging habits. Switching the unit to infrared camera mode avoids this issue. Black-and-white infrared night vision uses invisible light beams to film nighttime visitors clearly up to 98 feet away without frightening them. This passive approach supports ethical wildlife observation. Homeowners can observe natural behaviors without feeding animals, baiting them, or disrupting their regular travel routes. Precise video timestamps also help map local wildlife activity patterns. Logging the exact arrival times of visiting deer, mountain lions, or raccoons reveals recurring habits. Knowing these schedules allows us to bring pets indoors well before large predators begin their evening hunt. Two-way audio allows owners to listen to ambient forest sounds directly through a smartphone. If an unwelcome predator (animal or human) approaches, I can manually trigger a 110-decibel siren. The hardware connects over standard 2.4 gigahertz Wi-Fi networks. It does not connect over 5 gigahertz bands. The manufacturer notes the camera operates reliably between minus 4 degrees and 122 degrees Fahrenheit. An IP65 weather rating protects the electronics against driving rain, snow, and wind. Footage saves directly to a local Micro SD card holding up to 128 gigabytes. This local storage setup avoids monthly cloud fees while saving hours of midnight animal visits. An optional cloud trial is also available for 30 days. Deploying an infrared solar wildlife and security camera gives rural residents peace of mind. Homeowners gain a non-invasive window into natural wildlife habits while safeguarding their homestead with clean solar energy. So far, I am impressed and will be doing a video review on the Happy Eco News YouTube channel in the coming weeks. The cameras are available through Amazon or directly from SEHMUA online. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Buckwheat pillows offer a sustainable alternative to foam and polyester Reading Time: 3 minutes A farming byproduct that has filled pillows in Japan for generations is giving sleepers a plastic-free way to rest, and it can go back to the soil when it wears out. Every night, most of us rest our heads on a bag of plastic. Polyester fiber and memory foam, the two most common pillow fillings, are both made from fossil fuels. They clump, collect sweat and dust, and go flat within a year or two. Then the pillow gets thrown out. Most curbside recycling programs won’t take it, so it ends up in a landfill or an incinerator, and the cycle starts again with a new one. A growing number of sleepers are breaking that cycle with a leftover from buckwheat farming. A buckwheat pillow is filled with the hard outer shells of buckwheat seeds, the part nobody eats. Buckwheat is grown for its seeds, which are turned into flour, groats and noodles. Before the seed can be eaten, its tough, triangular shell has to be removed. Those shells, called hulls, are a byproduct of the milling process. Some are used for animal bedding or burned for fuel, but many have little value. Using hulls as pillow filling turns that waste stream into a useful product, in the same spirit as researchers turning leftover straw into crop waste fabric for clothing. No extra land is needed, because the hulls come from a crop that is already being grown for food. Pillows filled with buckwheat hulls have been used in Japan for generations, where they are known as sobakawa pillows. Their growing popularity in Europe and North America has more to do with materials: many shoppers now want a pillow that isn’t made from plastic. The crop itself also has a relatively light footprint. Buckwheat grows quickly, tolerates poor soils and generally needs little fertilizer. Its white flowers attract bees and other pollinators, and farmers often plant it as a cover crop to suppress weeds and protect the soil between other plantings. That doesn’t make every buckwheat pillow automatically green. Where the hulls are grown, how far they travel and how they are processed all make a difference. Hulls that are grown, milled and made into pillows in the same region carry far fewer transport emissions than those shipped across continents. No Fluff Pillow is one example of how short that supply chain can be. Its hulls come from a local buckwheat farm and are mechanically cleaned multiple times to remove dust and small particles. Each pillow is then filled by hand with 3.4 kg of hulls. Comfort is a big part of the appeal. Foam and polyester tend to trap heat, while hulls leave small air gaps between them so air keeps circulating. Many sleepers find that a buckwheat pillow stays noticeably cooler through the night. Buckwheat pillows also last much longer than conventional ones. Polyester fibers clump and foam gradually loses its shape, and neither can be repaired. Once they break down, the whole pillow has to be thrown away. Buckwheat hulls are hard and hold their shape for years. They slowly compress with use, and some break into smaller pieces, but owners can top the pillow up with fresh hulls or replace the filling entirely while keeping the same cover. Most buckwheat pillows also have a zipper, so sleepers can add or remove hulls to adjust height and firmness. One pillow can suit back, side and stomach sleepers, and a change in sleeping position doesn’t require a new purchase. When a buckwheat pillow finally does reach the end of its life, very little of it has to be thrown away. The hulls are plant material and can be added to a home compost pile or a yard waste bin, where they break down and return nutrients to the soil. Gardeners also use them as mulch. The cotton cover can be washed and reused, cut into cleaning cloths or taken to a textile collection point. A foam pillow, by contrast, has no practical recycling route in most places and can take decades to break down. Lawmakers are starting to take notice. California’s SB 707, the first statewide textile recycling law in the US, now covers pillows and bedding, and every EU country must set up similar producer-funded schemes for textiles by 2028. Buckwheat pillows do come with trade-offs. They are much heavier than fiber pillows, often weighing several kilograms. They are firm, molding to the head and neck rather than squashing flat, and most people need a few nights to adjust. They also rustle softly whenever the sleeper moves, a sound most people stop noticing within a week. Shoppers considering the switch can check where the hulls were grown and milled, how thoroughly they were cleaned, whether the cover is made from natural fibers such as organic cotton, and whether the pillow can be refilled rather than replaced. For households already composting food scraps or cutting back on plastic, the pillow is one of the easier swaps to make. The post Buckwheat pillows offer a sustainable alternative to foam and polyester appeared first on Happy Eco News .
